tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

entries.name: SendUserFile
entries.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

content.text:
Agreed on the split — and the branch points are few (the schema enum, `closet-grid.tsx`'s filter, `ALWAYS_REWEARABLE` in packing, and `by.Accessories` in the builder), so it's a contained change.

The reason it deserves a **category** rather than just a subcategory is that carried and worn items behave differently in three separate mechanisms, and categories are how this codebase expresses slots:

- **Cap** — you carry one bag, but you can wear a watch *and* a bracelet. Separate slots let each have its own limit instead of sharing the accessory budget.
- **Colour** — a tote is a large visible block that should count toward the 3-colour ceiling; a watch is a point, an accent at most. Right now they're scored identically.
- **Packing** — a bag is packed once for a trip, not per outfit. `ALWAYS_REWEARABLE` already gropes at this distinction with a hardcoded string set.

Two things I genuinely can't settle from your message, and they change what I build:

questions.question: You said "if we have watches, we should put them" — how strongly should a watch be worn?

options.label: Always, if owned
options.description: A watch is added to every look automatically and doesn't consume the accessory budget. Matches how people actually dress — you put your watch on daily without deciding. Strongest reading of what you said.

options.label: Strongly preferred
options.description: The scorer rewards looks that include a watch, so it usually appears but can be dropped when something else fits better. Softer, and consistent with how the generator treats every other preference (leans, not filters).

options.label: Just eligible
options.description: A watch competes for the accessory slots like a bracelet or scarf. Simplest — no new mechanism — but then nothing changes for watches specifically.

questions.question: Should bags/wallets be styled into generated outfits, or only live in the closet?

options.label: Own slot, max 1
options.description: A look can carry one bag, scored on colour like a real garment. The generator picks which bag suits the outfit.

options.label: Closet only
options.description: Catalogued and packable, but never shown in a generated look. Keeps the daily drop about clothing; a wallet in a look is noise.

options.label: Bags yes, wallets no
options.description: Visible carried items (tote, camera bag, backpack) get styled; a wallet is catalogued but never shown, since nobody sees it.

content.text:
Agreed on the substance, with one correction that matters: **don't key it off gender** — that's your own rule (rules key off the garment, since womenswear is extra garment types, not a switch). And you don't need to: the garment-keyed version produces exactly the outcome you described.

A steel sports watch against an evening dress is a *formality* mismatch (watch ≈ 2–3, dress ≈ 5), and `formalityCoherence` already sees that. A tailored menswear look sits at 3–4, where the same watch is coherent. So "almost always for a man, think twice with a dress" falls out of the numbers rather than being hardcoded — and it keeps working for a man in a tuxedo, which a gender switch would get wrong.

So the mechanism is your option 2, done as a **reward that a bad match outweighs**: a watch earns a bonus for being present, but a mismatched one loses more on coherence than the bonus is worth, so the generator simply omits it. Exactly your "we don't have another one, so we wouldn't give that watch." I'll verify those two numbers actually order that way rather than assuming.

**On bags, my recommendation: own slot, max 1.** Not the wallets-no variant — because your own item is called "Clutch wallet," and a clutch *is* a styled, visible piece. A rule that filters on the word "wallet" would misclassify it. The honest caveat: I called that item noise earlier, and I can't tell from the name whether it's an evening clutch or a billfold.  * nine live calls, Haiku never once picked the echoing combo over its

 * garment".** `echoScore` scores three-or-more echo points at 0.25 — the worst
 * outcome it can return — while the prompt tells the model a stated echo is

0.5000  accents=[]      navy top + navy trousers          ← correct: tonal dressing, no reward

gh pr create --base develop --head feat/scoring-foundations \

  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Groundwork for the remaining styling research. Each item here was blocking a
later rule, or was a defect found while clearing the way for one.

## Why

The reported bug was an outfit that picked a cream sneaker over one whose
swoosh echoed the shirt. Fixing the colour model exposed that several signals
could not be added at all: the weight budget could not accept a new term
without silently shrinking the others, a dead term was still claiming weight,
and `accent_color` was written by the tagger but read by nothing in the
generator.

## What changed

**Scoring**
- Weights are additive: each signal declares what it claims and the score
  normalises over what actually had evidence. Previously a new term had to be
  carved out of a base, so adding one changed every existing weight — with both
  preferences active, colour's real weight had fallen to 0.231.
- Deleted the `dna` term, which never fired. Verified rankings identical.
- A garment's `accent_color` reaches the colour model again. Measured on the
  real closet: pre-fix `{white, sky}` scored 1.0000 while post-fix
  `{white} + accent sky` scored 0.9025 — a plain white sneaker outranked the
  one with the blue swoosh.
- An accent is a **role, not a palette class**. Navy stays a neutral colour, but
  a navy swoosh on a white sneaker counts as an accent and may echo a navy top,
  while navy top + navy trousers stays tonal dressing and earns nothing.
  50 of 750 combos changed, all upward; the top 10 did not move.
- The re-ranker is handed the computed echo rather than asked to notice it.
  Live: the echoing combo was picked 6/6, against 0/9 before.

**Capture**
- `fit_source` records whether a fit was answered by a human or drafted by the
  model, so later proportion rules can weigh a real answer differently from a
  guess.
- `fit` and `length` are only asked for on garments worn on a body. A sneaker
  has neither, and a fit recorded against one inflated the count of items
  carrying a real fit.
- One definition of which categories are wearable, instead of three identical
  copies that could only disagree once a category was added.

**Looks**
- A look may carry two accessories, from different subcategories. The cap was a
  boolean gate before, so raising the number alone would have changed nothing.
  The candidate budget is unchanged: on the real closet, 154 combos at both
  caps, 38 of them now carrying two.

## Verification

- 1003 unit tests, `tsc` clean, `npm run build` clean, `npm run insights` clean.
- The fit-provenance path driven through the real UI at phone width: accepting
  the draft records `model`, tapping a chip records `user`, editing records
  `user`, clearing records neither.
- The category gate driven through the real edit sheet against a production
  build: an item carrying `fit=Oversized, fit_source=user, length=Cropped`
  saved as Shoes comes back with all three null.

## Review findings fixed in this branch

- Tonal dressing could buy the echo reward: a garment tagged with an
  `accent_color` equal to its own colour scored 1.0000 and was announced as a
  deliberate echo, where the same outfit without the redundant tag correctly
  scored 0.5000. A navy logo on a navy shirt is not a placement.
- The accessory coverage test proved nothing — it compared two caps on a closet
  producing 4 combos against a cap of 200. Rewritten so the cap binds; verified
  by introducing the regression and watching it fail.
- Two `CandidateItem` producers did not carry `subcategory`, safe only because
  of a constant several files away.

## Known limitations

- `camel/beige/camel` scores above `camel/black/black`, which the research
  endorses. Pairwise averaging cannot see a muddy trio; the value-contrast term
  and texture rescue that fix it are the next plan.
- Packing still allows one accessory per outfit, deliberately — a suitcase pays
  a cost a wardrobe does not.
- A closet with one top, one bottom and one shoe never reaches a second
  accessory. Pinned in a test.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

To be precise about what "all bugs fixed" means here: I fixed every defect my review found, and I closed the one verification gap that was outstanding. message.content: so we need more tests?

content.text:
No — the problem wasn't quantity. 1003 tests didn't prevent either finding, and one of them *was* a test.

The two failures had different causes:

**The echo bug** — no number of tests finds this. Nobody had asked "what if `accent_color` equals a colour the garment already has?" It's an unimagined input, and tests only cover imagined ones. That's what review is for, or better, making the state unrepresentable.

**The vacuous test** — more tests would have made this *worse*. It was a green check that guarded nothing, which is more dangerous than no test, because it buys false confidence.

So what's actually worth adopting is one habit, not more coverage: **for any test written to guard a specific regression, break the code and confirm it goes red before trusting it.** That's what caught both problems here — I injected the third `push` and watched the test still pass. It costs about thirty seconds and it's the only thing that distinguishes a real guard from a decoration.

One optional follow-up, if you want the echo class shut properly rather than defended: null an `accent_color` that duplicates one of the item's own colours at *write* time too, in `tagsToItemRow`. Right now `withAccent` defends against it on every read, which is correct and has to stay for existing rows — but writing clean data means the edit sheet stops offering a redundant accent in the first place. Small, and it's the "make the bad state impossible" version of the same fix. Say the word and I'll do it; it's not required for anything currently planned.

content.content:
1	# FitCheck — Accessories, Headwear, Scarves, and Base Layers
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	This is the unified FitCheck specification for accessories and base layers: belts, watches, bags, chains, necklaces, rings, earrings, bracelets, glasses, scarves, headwear, ties, pocket squares, socks, women's underwear, men's undershirts, tights, and intentionally visible base layers.
6	
7	The goal is to score more than colour matching. Each item may have a specific visual function:
8	
9	1. `leatherCoordination` — shoes, belt, watch strap, and sometimes bag.
10	2. `metalCoordination` — gold, silver, steel, brass, titanium, and dark hardware.
11	3. `accentEcho` — intentional repetition of a small colour detail between items.
12	4. `materialFormality` — material, finish, and visual weight versus dress code.
13	5. `statementBalance` — control of bold or high-visual-weight accessories.
14	6. `visualClutterPenalty` — protection from overloaded looks.
15	7. `baseLayerConcealment` — invisibility of underwear when it should not show.
16	8. `intentionalVisibility` — visible underwear only in an appropriate style register.
17	9. `hatScarfOuterHarmony` — compatibility of hats and scarves with outerwear.
18	
19	Accessories are structural outfit components: a belt connects lower and footwear; a watch connects leather, metal, and formality; a bag may be a large colour block; chains, earrings, and glasses draw attention near the face; scarves and hats can carry the whole accent band.[web:126][web:131][web:133][web:141][web:143][web:149][web:153]
20	
21	---
22	
23	## Core Principle: Palette Class Is Not Visual Role
24	
25	A colour should not have a single fixed role.
26	
27	- `navy`, `brown`, `camel`, `tan`, `denim`, `black`, and `grey` can be `palette neutrals`. This supports palette logic and the 3-colour ceiling.
28	- The same hue can be a `semantic accent` on a specific item when it occupies a small contrasting area or is intentionally repeated elsewhere.
29	
30	Examples:
31	
32	- A brown jacket is a primary neutral; a brown logo on a white sneaker is an accent.
33	- A navy shirt is a primary neutral; a navy swoosh or heel tab is an accent.
34	- A camel coat is a primary outer layer; a camel bag tab is an accent.
35	- Silver is a metal tone of a watch case, chain, ring, or buckle rather than simply a grey garment colour.
36	
37	```ts
38	type PaletteColorClass = "neutral" | "accent";
39	type VisualColorRole = "primary" | "secondary" | "detail" | "accent";
40	```
41	
42	Use `PaletteColorClass` for colour counting and the 3-colour ceiling. Use `VisualColorRole` for accent echo, dominant/secondary proportions, and accessory scoring.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## Recommended Data Model
47	
48	```ts
49	type AccessoryRole =
50	  | "belt"
51	  | "watch"
52	  | "bag"
53	  | "chain"
54	  | "necklace"
55	  | "ring"
56	  | "earrings"
57	  | "bracelet"
58	  | "scarf"
59	  | "hat"
60	  | "glasses"
61	  | "tie"
62	  | "pocket_square"
63	  | "socks"
64	  | "other";
65	
66	type AccessoryMaterial =
67	  | "Leather"
68	  | "Suede"
69	  | "Faux leather"
70	  | "Canvas"
71	  | "Cotton"
72	  | "Wool"
73	  | "Cashmere"
74	  | "Silk"
75	  | "Denim"
76	  | "Nylon"
77	  | "Polyester"
78	  | "Rubber"
79	  | "Stainless steel"
80	  | "Silver"
81	  | "Gold"
82	  | "Other";
83	
84	type MetalTone =
85	  | "cool" // silver, stainless steel, platinum, titanium, white gold
86	  | "warm" // yellow gold, rose gold, brass, copper
87	  | "dark" // black metal, gunmetal
88	  | "mixed"
89	  | "none";
90	
91	type Finish =
92	  | "matte"
93	  | "brushed"
94	  | "polished"
95	  | "shiny"
96	  | "textured"
97	  | "other";
98	
99	type VisualWeight = "low" | "medium" | "high";
100	type StatementLevel = "none" | "subtle" | "statement";
101	
102	type Accessory = {
103	  role: AccessoryRole;
104	  primaryColor?: Color;
105	  accentColors?: Color[];
106	  primaryColorRole?: "primary" | "secondary" | "detail" | "accent";
107	  material: AccessoryMaterial;
108	  metalTone?: MetalTone;
109	  finish?: Finish;
110	  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
111	  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
112	  statementLevel: StatementLevel;
113	  hasVisibleLogo?: boolean;
114	  isLeatherFamilyCarrier?: boolean;
115	};
116	```
117	
118	| Field | Why it is needed |
119	|---|---|
120	| `primaryColor` | A bag, belt, scarf, glasses frame, or watch strap can be a meaningful colour block |
121	| `accentColors` | A logo, buckle, sneaker detail, dial detail, gem, or hardware may create accent echo |
122	| `material` | Leather, nylon, silk, rubber, and canvas carry different formality signals |
123	| `metalTone` | Gold, silver, and steel are metal systems rather than ordinary clothing colours |
124	| `finish` | Polished leather/metal usually reads more formal than matte rubber/canvas |
125	| `visualWeight` | A thin chain and a heavy chain should not score identically |
126	| `statementLevel` | Needed to prevent visual clutter |
127	
128	---
129	
130	# Accessories
131	
132	## Accessory Roles
133	
134	| Role | Main visual function | Main checks |
135	|---|---|---|
136	| `belt` | Connects lower and footwear; creates a waist break | Leather family, buckle metal, formality |
137	| `watch` | Connects leather, metal, and dress code | Strap, case metal, dial, visual weight |
138	| `bag` | Neutral anchor, echo, or statement | Colour intent, material, hardware, scale |
139	| `chain` / `necklace` | Metal accent near the face | Metal family, thickness, statement balance |
140	| `ring` | Repeats watch/chain metal tone | Metal family, count, visual weight |
141	| `earrings` | High-visibility face-level accent | Metal, stone colour, size |
142	| `bracelet` | May echo watch strap or metal | Material, metal family, overlap with watch |
143	| `scarf` | Strong colour carrier near the face | Echo, pattern load, season/material |
144	| `hat` | Supports or accents outerwear | Colour, material weight, register |
145	| `glasses` | High-visibility facial detail | Frame colour, hardware, formality |
146	| `tie` | Formal accent band | Colour echo, pattern, texture |
147	| `pocket_square` | Echoes tie/outfit without exact duplication | Secondary-colour extraction |
148	| `socks` | Connect lower to footwear or carry a small accent | Trouser relation, pattern load |
149	
150	---
151	
152	## Leather Coordination: Footwear, Belt, Watch, and Bag
153	
154	### Core Rule
155	
156	In classic menswear and business outfits, shoes and belt should use the same leather colour family. A leather watch strap normally follows that family. This is family coordination rather than exact RGB matching: black with black, dark brown with dark brown, tan/cognac with tan/cognac/brown.[web:126][web:131][web:132][web:133][web:141][web:143][web:151]
157	
158	```ts
159	type LeatherFamily =
160	  | "black"
161	  | "dark_brown"
162	  | "medium_brown"
163	  | "tan_cognac"
164	  | "burgundy_oxblood"
165	  | "grey"
166	  | "white_cream"
167	  | "other";
168	```
169	
170	| Footwear | Belt | Leather watch strap | Classic/business result |
171	|---|---|---|---|
172	| Black | Black | Black | Canonical |
173	| Dark brown | Dark brown | Dark brown | Canonical |
174	| Dark brown | Medium brown | Dark brown | Good; same family |
175	| Tan/cognac | Tan/cognac | Brown/tan | Good; smart-casual leaning |
176	| Burgundy/oxblood | Burgundy/dark brown | Burgundy/dark brown | Good with control |
177	| Brown | Black | Any | Avoid |
178	| Black | Brown | Any | Avoid |
179	| White sneakers | No belt or neutral belt | Casual strap | Register-dependent |
180	
181	### Scoring
182	
183	| Rule | Classic/business | Smart casual | Streetwear |
184	|---|---:|---:|---:|
185	| Shoes and belt share leather family | +10 | +6 | +2 |
186	| Shoes and belt are close brown shades | +8 | +6 | +3 |
187	| Leather strap follows shoe/belt family | +6 | +4 | +1 |
188	| Brown shoes with black belt | -15 | -9 | -4 |
189	| Black shoes with brown belt | -15 | -9 | -4 |
190	| Leather strap clashes with shoes/belt | -6 | -3 | -1 |
191	| Canvas/rubber/NATO strap with formal tailoring | -8 | -2 | 0 |
192	| Canvas/rubber/NATO strap with streetwear/techwear | 0 | +3 | +6 |
193	
194	`black shoes + black belt + black leather strap` is leather cohesion, not necessarily accent echo. A `white sneaker + brown logo + brown jacket` can count as accent echo because the brown footwear detail repeats a dominant outer colour.
195	
196	---
197	
198	## Watches
199	
200	```ts
201	type Watch = {
202	  strapMaterial: AccessoryMaterial;
203	  strapColor?: Color;
204	  caseMetalTone: MetalTone;
205	  dialColor?: Color;
206	  dialAccentColors?: Color[];
207	  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
208	  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
209	};
210	```
211	
212	### Assessment Order
213	
214	1. Strap material versus outfit register.
215	2. Leather strap colour versus belt and shoes.
216	3. Case metal versus rings, chain, earrings, and buckle.
217	4. Dial colour as a low-weight optional colour echo.
218	
219	| Strap | Formal | Business | Smart casual | Casual/streetwear |
220	|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
221	| Thin black leather | 5 | 5 | 3 | 1 |
222	| Brown leather | 4–5 | 4 | 3 | 1 |
223	| Stainless-steel bracelet | 3–4 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
224	| Rubber | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 4 |
225	| NATO / Nylon | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 4 |
226	| Canvas/Fabric | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 3 |
227	
228	Leather straps are formal/business defaults; steel is normally business-safe; rubber, nylon, and fabric suit casual, athletic, technical, and streetwear registers.[web:141][web:142][web:143][web:146][web:151]
229	
230	A navy dial with a navy knit can receive a small echo bonus if the dial is visible and the outfit has no noisy accent system. It must not become a hard requirement.
231	
232	---
233	
234	## Metals: Gold, Silver, Steel, Titanium, Brass, and Gunmetal
235	
236	| Metal family | Includes | General style signal |
237	|---|---|---|
238	| Cool | Silver, stainless steel, platinum, titanium, white gold | Clean, cool, modern, neutral |
239	| Warm | Yellow gold, rose gold, brass, copper | Warm, rich, earthy, dressy |
240	| Dark | Black metal, gunmetal | Streetwear, technical, dark minimal |
241	| Mixed | Two intentional families | Requires dominant metal plus repetition |
242	
243	### Core Rule
244	
245	The safest classic/business approach is one visible metal family: steel watch + silver chain + silver rings + silver buckle, or gold earrings + gold chain + gold rings + gold hardware. Modern styling accepts mixed metals when one metal clearly leads and the secondary metal is limited and repeated.[web:127][web:128][web:129][web:130][web:134][web:135][web:137][web:140][web:172][web:173]
246	
247	| Scenario | Score | Rule type |
248	|---|---:|---|
249	| One visible metal family across watch/jewellery/hardware | +10 | STRONG |
250	| Cool system: steel/silver/titanium | +8 | STRONG |
251	| Warm system: gold/brass/rose gold | +8 | STRONG |
252	| Mixed metals; dominant about 70%; secondary repeats at least twice | +5 | PREFERENCE/STRONG |
253	| Two-tone watch connects both metals | +4 | PREFERENCE |
254	| One gold item + one silver item, with no repeat | 0 | Neutral |
255	| Gold watch + silver chain + steel rings + brass buckle | -8 | STRONG penalty |
256	
257	### Metal Versus Clothing Palette
258	
259	This is a preference, not a filter:
260	
261	| Garment palette | Preferred metal |
262	|---|---|
263	| Navy, charcoal, grey, black, silver | Cool metal |
264	| Camel, tan, brown, rust, olive, mustard | Warm metal |
265	| Black techwear, nylon, black hardware | Dark metal or cool steel |
266	| Mixed neutrals | Any internally consistent metal family |
267	
268	Gold with navy and silver with camel should not be prohibited. Consistency across visible metal elements is more reliable than a direct metal-to-garment rule.[web:128][web:138][web:139]
269	
270	---
271	
272	## Chains, Rings, Earrings, and Bracelets
273	
274	### Metal Echo
275	
276	`metalEcho` is a repeated metal family across meaningful accessories:
277	
278	- Steel watch + silver chain + silver ring.
279	- Gold earrings + gold necklace + gold bracelet.
280	- Black watch case + gunmetal chain + black bag hardware.
281	
282	```ts
283	function hasMetalEcho(items: Accessory[]): boolean {
284	  return countRepeatedMetalFamily(items) >= 2;
285	}
286	```
287	
288	### Visual Weight and Statement Balance
289	
290	| Item | Low | Medium | High / statement |
291	|---|---|---|---|
292	| Chain | Thin chain | Medium pendant | Thick chain / large pendant |
293	| Ring | One slim ring | 2–3 rings | Multiple chunky rings |
294	| Earrings | Studs | Small hoops | Large hoops / bright gems |
295	| Bracelet | Thin metal/leather | Watch + bracelet | Multiple stacked bracelets |
296	| Watch | Thin dress watch | Standard steel watch | Large diver/sport watch |
297	
298	Rules:
299	
300	- STRONG: only one high-statement accessory should be the main focal point.
301	- STRONG: a statement chain requires quieter rings, earrings, and bracelets.
302	- STRONG: a bold watch plus thick chain plus chunky rings plus bright scarf is visual clutter.
303	- PREFERENCE: repeat one metal tone in two or three accessories without using identical scale and shape everywhere.[web:126][web:128][web:129][web:130][web:135][web:136][web:140][web:171][web:172]
304	
305	---
306	
307	## Bags
308	
309	```ts
310	type BagIntent = "blend" | "echo" | "contrast";
311	```
312	
313	| Intent | When to use | Example |
314	|---|---|---|
315	| `blend` | Shoes or outerwear already makes a statement | Black bag with black/grey/navy outfit |
316	| `echo` | Need to connect shoes, belt, outerwear, or scarf | Brown leather bag echoes brown shoes/belt |
317	| `contrast` | Neutral outfit needs one focal point | Burgundy bag with navy/grey base |
318	
319	Rules:
320	
321	- In business/classic outfits, material and formality matter more than exact bag colour.
322	- Exact shoe-bag matching is safe but not mandatory.
323	- Modern default: coordinate by colour family, undertone, finish, material, or one repeated hardware detail.
324	- Statement footwear suggests a neutral/tonal bag.
325	- A neutral outfit can use the bag as one accent carrier.
326	- Bright bag + bright scarf + bright hat is usually clutter.[web:149][web:150][web:152][web:153][web:169][web:170][web:171]
327	
328	| Outfit | Bag | Result |
329	|---|---|---|
330	| Navy suit + dark-brown shoes + dark-brown belt | Dark-brown leather bag | +8 leather/formality cohesion |
331	| Black outfit + black boots | Black structured bag | +7 blend / column continuation |
332	| Camel coat + denim + white sneakers | Camel/tan bag | +5 outer echo |
333	| Camel coat + denim + white sneakers | Bright red bag + red scarf + red hat | -8 clutter |
334	| Black technical shell + black sneakers | Black nylon crossbody | +6 material/register alignment |
335	
336	---
337	
338	## Ties, Pocket Squares, Socks, and Glasses
339	
340	### Tie and Pocket Square
341	
342	- A tie is usually the main formal accent.
343	- A pocket square should echo a secondary tie/outfit colour instead of replicating the exact tie fabric/pattern.
344	- Identical tie-and-pocket-square sets look pre-packaged and should receive a penalty.[web:118][web:119][web:124]
345	
346	```ts
347	if (tie.color === pocketSquare.color && tie.pattern === pocketSquare.pattern) {
348	  score -= OVERMATCHED_SET_PENALTY;
349	}
350	
351	if (pocketSquare.contains(tie.secondaryColor)) {
352	  score += SECONDARY_COLOR_ECHO_BONUS;
353	}
354	```
355	
356	### Socks
357	
358	- Classic default: socks follow the `lower` colour, not the footwear colour.
359	- Patterned socks are one controlled smart-casual accent.
360	- Loud socks + loud tie + loud square + loud shoes should receive a clutter penalty.
361	
362	### Glasses
363	
364	```ts
365	type Glasses = {
366	  frameColor?: Color;
367	  frameMaterial: "acetate" | "metal" | "mixed";
368	  metalTone?: MetalTone;
369	  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
370	  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
371	};
372	```
373	
374	- Black acetate can quietly echo black leather or dark outerwear.
375	- Tortoiseshell/brown can support brown leather, camel/tan, and earthy palettes.
376	- Silver metal frames can support cool metal systems.
377	- Frames do not need to match clothing; treat matching as a weak preference.
378	- Bright/thick frames are statement accessories and reduce the allowed statement load.
379	
380	---
381	
382	## Accent Echo Through Accessories
383	
384	Accessory echo earns a bonus only if all conditions are met:
385	
386	1. A colour is visibly a `detail` or `accent` on a source item.
387	2. The same hue/family appears as primary, secondary, or meaningful accent on another item.
388	3. The roles form a meaningful visible link.
389	4. The outfit has at most two strong accent hues.
390	5. The match is not a random pixel shared by overloaded multi-colour graphics.
391	
392	```ts
393	function qualifiesAsAccessoryEcho(
394	  source: GarmentOrAccessory,

# FitCheck — Accessories, Headwear, Scarves, and Base Layers

## Purpose

This is the unified FitCheck specification for accessories and base layers: belts, watches, bags, chains, necklaces, rings, earrings, bracelets, glasses, scarves, headwear, ties, pocket squares, socks, women's underwear, men's undershirts, tights, and intentionally visible base layers.

The goal is to score more than colour matching. Each item may have a specific visual function:

1. `leatherCoordination` — shoes, belt, watch strap, and sometimes bag.
2. `metalCoordination` — gold, silver, steel, brass, titanium, and dark hardware.
3. `accentEcho` — intentional repetition of a small colour detail between items.
4. `materialFormality` — material, finish, and visual weight versus dress code.
5. `statementBalance` — control of bold or high-visual-weight accessories.
6. `visualClutterPenalty` — protection from overloaded looks.
7. `baseLayerConcealment` — invisibility of underwear when it should not show.
8. `intentionalVisibility` — visible underwear only in an appropriate style register.
9. `hatScarfOuterHarmony` — compatibility of hats and scarves with outerwear.

Accessories are structural outfit components: a belt connects lower and footwear; a watch connects leather, metal, and formality; a bag may be a large colour block; chains, earrings, and glasses draw attention near the face; scarves and hats can carry the whole accent band.[web:126][web:131][web:133][web:141][web:143][web:149][web:153]

---

## Core Principle: Palette Class Is Not Visual Role

A colour should not have a single fixed role.

- `navy`, `brown`, `camel`, `tan`, `denim`, `black`, and `grey` can be `palette neutrals`. This supports palette logic and the 3-colour ceiling.
- The same hue can be a `semantic accent` on a specific item when it occupies a small contrasting area or is intentionally repeated elsewhere.

Examples:

- A brown jacket is a primary neutral; a brown logo on a white sneaker is an accent.
- A navy shirt is a primary neutral; a navy swoosh or heel tab is an accent.
- A camel coat is a primary outer layer; a camel bag tab is an accent.
- Silver is a metal tone of a watch case, chain, ring, or buckle rather than simply a grey garment colour.

```ts
type PaletteColorClass = "neutral" | "accent";
type VisualColorRole = "primary" | "secondary" | "detail" | "accent";
```

Use `PaletteColorClass` for colour counting and the 3-colour ceiling. Use `VisualColorRole` for accent echo, dominant/secondary proportions, and accessory scoring.

---

## Recommended Data Model

```ts
type AccessoryRole =
  | "belt"
  | "watch"
  | "bag"
  | "chain"
  | "necklace"
  | "ring"
  | "earrings"
  | "bracelet"
  | "scarf"
  | "hat"
  | "glasses"
  | "tie"
  | "pocket_square"
  | "socks"
  | "other";

type AccessoryMaterial =
  | "Leather"
  | "Suede"
  | "Faux leather"
  | "Canvas"
  | "Cotton"
  | "Wool"
  | "Cashmere"
  | "Silk"
  | "Denim"
  | "Nylon"
  | "Polyester"
  | "Rubber"
  | "Stainless steel"
  | "Silver"
  | "Gold"
  | "Other";

type MetalTone =
  | "cool" // silver, stainless steel, platinum, titanium, white gold
  | "warm" // yellow gold, rose gold, brass, copper
  | "dark" // black metal, gunmetal
  | "mixed"
  | "none";

type Finish =
  | "matte"
  | "brushed"
  | "polished"
  | "shiny"
  | "textured"
  | "other";

type VisualWeight = "low" | "medium" | "high";
type StatementLevel = "none" | "subtle" | "statement";

type Accessory = {
  role: AccessoryRole;
  primaryColor?: Color;
  accentColors?: Color[];
  primaryColorRole?: "primary" | "secondary" | "detail" | "accent";
  material: AccessoryMaterial;
  metalTone?: MetalTone;
  finish?: Finish;
  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
  statementLevel: StatementLevel;
  hasVisibleLogo?: boolean;
  isLeatherFamilyCarrier?: boolean;
};
```

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| `primaryColor` | A bag, belt, scarf, glasses frame, or watch strap can be a meaningful colour block |
| `accentColors` | A logo, buckle, sneaker detail, dial detail, gem, or hardware may create accent echo |
| `material` | Leather, nylon, silk, rubber, and canvas carry different formality signals |
| `metalTone` | Gold, silver, and steel are metal systems rather than ordinary clothing colours |
| `finish` | Polished leather/metal usually reads more formal than matte rubber/canvas |
| `visualWeight` | A thin chain and a heavy chain should not score identically |
| `statementLevel` | Needed to prevent visual clutter |

---

# Accessories

## Accessory Roles

| Role | Main visual function | Main checks |
|---|---|---|
| `belt` | Connects lower and footwear; creates a waist break | Leather family, buckle metal, formality |
| `watch` | Connects leather, metal, and dress code | Strap, case metal, dial, visual weight |
| `bag` | Neutral anchor, echo, or statement | Colour intent, material, hardware, scale |
| `chain` / `necklace` | Metal accent near the face | Metal family, thickness, statement balance |
| `ring` | Repeats watch/chain metal tone | Metal family, count, visual weight |
| `earrings` | High-visibility face-level accent | Metal, stone colour, size |
| `bracelet` | May echo watch strap or metal | Material, metal family, overlap with watch |
| `scarf` | Strong colour carrier near the face | Echo, pattern load, season/material |
| `hat` | Supports or accents outerwear | Colour, material weight, register |
| `glasses` | High-visibility facial detail | Frame colour, hardware, formality |
| `tie` | Formal accent band | Colour echo, pattern, texture |
| `pocket_square` | Echoes tie/outfit without exact duplication | Secondary-colour extraction |
| `socks` | Connect lower to footwear or carry a small accent | Trouser relation, pattern load |

---

## Leather Coordination: Footwear, Belt, Watch, and Bag

### Core Rule

In classic menswear and business outfits, shoes and belt should use the same leather colour family. A leather watch strap normally follows that family. This is family coordination rather than exact RGB matching: black with black, dark brown with dark brown, tan/cognac with tan/cognac/brown.[web:126][web:131][web:132][web:133][web:141][web:143][web:151]

```ts
type LeatherFamily =
  | "black"
  | "dark_brown"
  | "medium_brown"
  | "tan_cognac"
  | "burgundy_oxblood"
  | "grey"
  | "white_cream"
  | "other";
```

| Footwear | Belt | Leather watch strap | Classic/business result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Black | Black | Black | Canonical |
| Dark brown | Dark brown | Dark brown | Canonical |
| Dark brown | Medium brown | Dark brown | Good; same family |
| Tan/cognac | Tan/cognac | Brown/tan | Good; smart-casual leaning |
| Burgundy/oxblood | Burgundy/dark brown | Burgundy/dark brown | Good with control |
| Brown | Black | Any | Avoid |
| Black | Brown | Any | Avoid |
| White sneakers | No belt or neutral belt | Casual strap | Register-dependent |

### Scoring

| Rule | Classic/business | Smart casual | Streetwear |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Shoes and belt share leather family | +10 | +6 | +2 |
| Shoes and belt are close brown shades | +8 | +6 | +3 |
| Leather strap follows shoe/belt family | +6 | +4 | +1 |
| Brown shoes with black belt | -15 | -9 | -4 |
| Black shoes with brown belt | -15 | -9 | -4 |
| Leather strap clashes with shoes/belt | -6 | -3 | -1 |
| Canvas/rubber/NATO strap with formal tailoring | -8 | -2 | 0 |
| Canvas/rubber/NATO strap with streetwear/techwear | 0 | +3 | +6 |

`black shoes + black belt + black leather strap` is leather cohesion, not necessarily accent echo. A `white sneaker + brown logo + brown jacket` can count as accent echo because the brown footwear detail repeats a dominant outer colour.

---

## Watches

```ts
type Watch = {
  strapMaterial: AccessoryMaterial;
  strapColor?: Color;
  caseMetalTone: MetalTone;
  dialColor?: Color;
  dialAccentColors?: Color[];
  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
};
```

### Assessment Order

1. Strap material versus outfit register.
2. Leather strap colour versus belt and shoes.
3. Case metal versus rings, chain, earrings, and buckle.
4. Dial colour as a low-weight optional colour echo.

| Strap | Formal | Business | Smart casual | Casual/streetwear |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Thin black leather | 5 | 5 | 3 | 1 |
| Brown leather | 4–5 | 4 | 3 | 1 |
| Stainless-steel bracelet | 3–4 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| Rubber | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 4 |
| NATO / Nylon | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 4 |
| Canvas/Fabric | 1 | 1–2 | 2 | 3 |

Leather straps are formal/business defaults; steel is normally business-safe; rubber, nylon, and fabric suit casual, athletic, technical, and streetwear registers.[web:141][web:142][web:143][web:146][web:151]

A navy dial with a navy knit can receive a small echo bonus if the dial is visible and the outfit has no noisy accent system. It must not become a hard requirement.

---

## Metals: Gold, Silver, Steel, Titanium, Brass, and Gunmetal

| Metal family | Includes | General style signal |
|---|---|---|
| Cool | Silver, stainless steel, platinum, titanium, white gold | Clean, cool, modern, neutral |
| Warm | Yellow gold, rose gold, brass, copper | Warm, rich, earthy, dressy |
| Dark | Black metal, gunmetal | Streetwear, technical, dark minimal |
| Mixed | Two intentional families | Requires dominant metal plus repetition |

### Core Rule

The safest classic/business approach is one visible metal family: steel watch + silver chain + silver rings + silver buckle, or gold earrings + gold chain + gold rings + gold hardware. Modern styling accepts mixed metals when one metal clearly leads and the secondary metal is limited and repeated.[web:127][web:128][web:129][web:130][web:134][web:135][web:137][web:140][web:172][web:173]

| Scenario | Score | Rule type |
|---|---:|---|
| One visible metal family across watch/jewellery/hardware | +10 | STRONG |
| Cool system: steel/silver/titanium | +8 | STRONG |
| Warm system: gold/brass/rose gold | +8 | STRONG |
| Mixed metals; dominant about 70%; secondary repeats at least twice | +5 | PREFERENCE/STRONG |
| Two-tone watch connects both metals | +4 | PREFERENCE |
| One gold item + one silver item, with no repeat | 0 | Neutral |
| Gold watch + silver chain + steel rings + brass buckle | -8 | STRONG penalty |

### Metal Versus Clothing Palette

This is a preference, not a filter:

| Garment palette | Preferred metal |
|---|---|
| Navy, charcoal, grey, black, silver | Cool metal |
| Camel, tan, brown, rust, olive, mustard | Warm metal |
| Black techwear, nylon, black hardware | Dark metal or cool steel |
| Mixed neutrals | Any internally consistent metal family |

Gold with navy and silver with camel should not be prohibited. Consistency across visible metal elements is more reliable than a direct metal-to-garment rule.[web:128][web:138][web:139]

---

## Chains, Rings, Earrings, and Bracelets

### Metal Echo

`metalEcho` is a repeated metal family across meaningful accessories:

- Steel watch + silver chain + silver ring.
- Gold earrings + gold necklace + gold bracelet.
- Black watch case + gunmetal chain + black bag hardware.

```ts
function hasMetalEcho(items: Accessory[]): boolean {
  return countRepeatedMetalFamily(items) >= 2;
}
```

### Visual Weight and Statement Balance

| Item | Low | Medium | High / statement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chain | Thin chain | Medium pendant | Thick chain / large pendant |
| Ring | One slim ring | 2–3 rings | Multiple chunky rings |
| Earrings | Studs | Small hoops | Large hoops / bright gems |
| Bracelet | Thin metal/leather | Watch + bracelet | Multiple stacked bracelets |
| Watch | Thin dress watch | Standard steel watch | Large diver/sport watch |

Rules:

- STRONG: only one high-statement accessory should be the main focal point.
- STRONG: a statement chain requires quieter rings, earrings, and bracelets.
- STRONG: a bold watch plus thick chain plus chunky rings plus bright scarf is visual clutter.
- PREFERENCE: repeat one metal tone in two or three accessories without using identical scale and shape everywhere.[web:126][web:128][web:129][web:130][web:135][web:136][web:140][web:171][web:172]

---

## Bags

```ts
type BagIntent = "blend" | "echo" | "contrast";
```

| Intent | When to use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `blend` | Shoes or outerwear already makes a statement | Black bag with black/grey/navy outfit |
| `echo` | Need to connect shoes, belt, outerwear, or scarf | Brown leather bag echoes brown shoes/belt |
| `contrast` | Neutral outfit needs one focal point | Burgundy bag with navy/grey base |

Rules:

- In business/classic outfits, material and formality matter more than exact bag colour.
- Exact shoe-bag matching is safe but not mandatory.
- Modern default: coordinate by colour family, undertone, finish, material, or one repeated hardware detail.
- Statement footwear suggests a neutral/tonal bag.
- A neutral outfit can use the bag as one accent carrier.
- Bright bag + bright scarf + bright hat is usually clutter.[web:149][web:150][web:152][web:153][web:169][web:170][web:171]

| Outfit | Bag | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Navy suit + dark-brown shoes + dark-brown belt | Dark-brown leather bag | +8 leather/formality cohesion |
| Black outfit + black boots | Black structured bag | +7 blend / column continuation |
| Camel coat + denim + white sneakers | Camel/tan bag | +5 outer echo |
| Camel coat + denim + white sneakers | Bright red bag + red scarf + red hat | -8 clutter |
| Black technical shell + black sneakers | Black nylon crossbody | +6 material/register alignment |

---

## Ties, Pocket Squares, Socks, and Glasses

### Tie and Pocket Square

- A tie is usually the main formal accent.
- A pocket square should echo a secondary tie/outfit colour instead of replicating the exact tie fabric/pattern.
- Identical tie-and-pocket-square sets look pre-packaged and should receive a penalty.[web:118][web:119][web:124]

```ts
if (tie.color === pocketSquare.color && tie.pattern === pocketSquare.pattern) {
  score -= OVERMATCHED_SET_PENALTY;
}

if (pocketSquare.contains(tie.secondaryColor)) {
  score += SECONDARY_COLOR_ECHO_BONUS;
}
```

### Socks

- Classic default: socks follow the `lower` colour, not the footwear colour.
- Patterned socks are one controlled smart-casual accent.
- Loud socks + loud tie + loud square + loud shoes should receive a clutter penalty.

### Glasses

```ts
type Glasses = {
  frameColor?: Color;
  frameMaterial: "acetate" | "metal" | "mixed";
  metalTone?: MetalTone;
  visualWeight: VisualWeight;
  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
};
```

- Black acetate can quietly echo black leather or dark outerwear.
- Tortoiseshell/brown can support brown leather, camel/tan, and earthy palettes.
- Silver metal frames can support cool metal systems.
- Frames do not need to match clothing; treat matching as a weak preference.
- Bright/thick frames are statement accessories and reduce the allowed statement load.

---

## Accent Echo Through Accessories

Accessory echo earns a bonus only if all conditions are met:

1. A colour is visibly a `detail` or `accent` on a source item.
2. The same hue/family appears as primary, secondary, or meaningful accent on another item.
3. The roles form a meaningful visible link.
4. The outfit has at most two strong accent hues.
5. The match is not a random pixel shared by overloaded multi-colour graphics.

```ts
function qualifiesAsAccessoryEcho(
  source: GarmentOrAccessory,
  target: GarmentOrAccessory,
  outfit: Outfit
): boolean {
  return (
    source.hasVisibleAccentColor &&
    colorFamilyMatch(source.accentColor, target.primaryOrAccentColor) &&
    isMeaningfulRoleConnection(source.role, target.role) &&
    countStrongAccentHues(outfit) <= 2 &&
    !isNoiseFromMulticolorPrint(source, target)
  );
}
```

| Source role | Target role | Echo weight |
|---|---|---:|
| Footwear detail | Upper primary/secondary | High |
| Footwear detail | Outer primary/secondary | High |
| Bag | Outer/scarf/footwear | Medium-high |
| Tie | Pocket square | High in formal register |
| Scarf | Footwear/bag/outer | Medium-high |
| Watch dial | Upper/outer | Low-medium |
| Ring/earring gem | Top/scarf/bag | Low-medium |
| Tiny print detail | Tiny logo on another item | Low / usually zero |

### Echo That Should Trigger

| Outfit | Echo | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Navy top + white pants + white AF1 with navy swoosh | Navy swoosh ↔ navy top | Clear footwear-to-upper link |
| Camel coat + denim + white sneakers with camel heel tab | Camel tab ↔ camel outer | Clear footwear-to-outer echo |
| Grey tee + tan chinos + white sneaker with tan stripe | Tan stripe ↔ tan lower | Controlled lower-footwear relation |
| White sneaker with brown logo + brown jacket | Brown logo ↔ brown outer | Detail repeats dominant outer hue |
| Navy suit + burgundy tie + white square with burgundy border | Tie ↔ square | Formal secondary-colour echo |
| Steel watch + silver chain + silver ring | Metal echo | Intentional cool-metal system |

### Echo That Should Not Trigger

| Outfit | Why |
|---|---|
| Multi-colour graphic tee + multi-colour sneaker with random shared blue | Coincidental colour noise |
| All-navy top + navy trousers + navy sneakers | Tonal/monochrome, not accent echo |
| Brown suit + brown shirt + brown tie + brown shoes | Tonal dressing; avoid double count |
| Gold watch + single silver ring without repeated silver | Weak accidental mixed-metal relation |
| Bright red bag + red scarf + red cap + red shoe detail | Overmatched / too many accent carriers |
| Black belt with brown shoes because watch dial is black | Dial cannot rescue leather clash |

---

## 3-Colour Ceiling and Accessories

Accessories should not automatically break the 3-colour ceiling.

- Palette count includes major visible colour families.
- A small accessory detail that repeats an existing hue does not create a new full colour slot.
- A new bright statement bag, scarf, or hat normally counts as a separate accent hue.

| Outfit | Palette count | Logic |
|---|---:|---|
| Navy top + white pants + white shoe with navy swoosh | 2 | Navy detail is echo, not a new colour |
| Camel coat + denim + white sneaker with camel tab | 3 | Tab does not add a new hue |
| Grey suit + black shoes/belt + silver watch | 2–3 | Silver hardware is normally not garment hue |
| Navy/grey + burgundy tie + burgundy bag | 3 | One repeated accent hue |
| Navy/grey + burgundy tie + mustard scarf + red bag | 5 | Too many accents; penalty |

---

# Hats, Scarves, and Outerwear

## Hat/Scarf as an Outerwear System

Hats and scarves sit close to the face and should be treated as a coordinated system with `outer`. They can `blend`, create `echo`, or serve as one controlled `statement`. In winter, a coat is frequently the largest visible colour block; hats and scarves should support it or contrast intentionally rather than compete with it.[web:174][web:175][web:177][web:183][web:186]

```ts
type HatType =
  | "beanie"
  | "cap"
  | "bucket"
  | "fedora"
  | "flat_cap"
  | "beret"
  | "wool_hat"
  | "fur_hat"
  | "balaclava"
  | "other";

type ScarfType =
  | "long_rectangular"
  | "square"
  | "infinity"
  | "narrow_silk"
  | "chunky_knit"
  | "cashmere"
  | "wool"
  | "linen"
  | "other";
```

## Hat Types

| Hat type | Register | Typical material | Formality |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Beanie | Casual, streetwear, winter casual | Wool, Cashmere, Acrylic, Cotton | 1–3 |
| Baseball/dad cap | Casual, streetwear, athleisure | Cotton, Canvas, Nylon | 1–2 |
| Bucket | Streetwear, casual summer | Cotton, Nylon, Canvas | 1–2 |
| Flat cap | Smart casual, classic, heritage | Wool, Tweed, Cotton | 3–4 |
| Fedora | Smart casual, fashion, classic | Wool/Felt | 3–4 |

524	|---|---|---|
525	| Wool overcoat | Wool/cashmere beanie, flat cap, structured wool hat | Thin summer cotton cap |
526	| Puffer | Knit beanie, technical cap, fleece hat | Formal felt fedora |
527	| Parka | Wool beanie, fleece/technical hat | Light silk system |
528	| Trench | Beret, flat cap, light wool hat, structured cap | Heavy chunky beanie |

534	Hat fabric weight should match coat weight and season.[web:175][web:176][web:186]

536	## Scarf and Coat Rules
537	
538	1. The coat leads the outfit; a bold coat requires a quieter scarf.
539	2. A slim tailored coat works best with a narrow/medium scarf; puffers and parkas can carry chunkier knit/fleece.
540	3. Scarf material must align with season and coat formality.
541	4. An accent scarf works best when it repeats in one other meaningful item: bag, shoes, hat, gloves, or tie.[web:177][web:179][web:181][web:183][web:184]
542	
543	| Coat type | Recommended scarf | Avoid |
544	|---|---|---|
545	| Trench | Medium Cotton, Silk, Fine Wool | Oversized chunky knit/infinity |
546	| Wool peacoat | Thin ribbed knit, Wool, Cashmere | Very bulky double wrap |
547	| Wool overcoat | Cashmere, Fine Wool, structured knit | Fleece/sports scarf/loud novelty knit |
548	| Puffer | Long flat scarf, Chunky knit, Fleece | Thin silk as a winter layer |
549	| Parka | Wool, Fleece, Chunky knit | Formal silk in outdoor setting |
550	| Cape/cocoon | Slender/tucked scarf | Stiff bulky scarf |
551	| Leather jacket | Fine Wool, Cotton, light knit | Overly formal fur scarf in casual register |
552	| Denim jacket | Cotton/light Wool/casual knit | Heavy cashmere in warm weather |
553	
554	| Scenario | Result | Rule strength |
555	|---|---:|---|
556	| Scarf 1–2 shades lighter/darker than coat | +4 | STRONG |
557	| Neutral scarf with neutral coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
558	| Camel scarf + navy coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
559	| Grey scarf + camel coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
560	| Burgundy/olive/rust scarf repeated in bag/shoes/hat | +5 | STRONG |
561	| Bright scarf is the single bright accent | +2 | PREFERENCE |
562	| Bright scarf + bright hat + bright bag | -8 | HARD/STRONG penalty |
563	| Patterned scarf uses outfit palette | +3 | PREFERENCE |
564	| Patterned scarf adds 3–4 new colours | -4 | STRONG penalty |
565	| Colourful coat + neutral scarf | +4 | STRONG |
566	| Colourful coat + unrelated equally bright scarf | -5 | STRONG penalty |
567	
568	## Hat and Scarf Together
569	
570	Only one should be a strong statement accessory in normal classic, business, or smart-casual winter outfits.
571	
572	| Hat | Scarf | Result |
573	|---|---|---|
574	| Neutral/tonal | Bright/patterned but echoed elsewhere | Good |
575	| Bright/patterned but echoed in shoes | Neutral/tonal | Good |
576	| Same family, different shades/textures | Good tonal system |
577	| Exact same colour + material | Flat / overly matched |
578	| Bright red | Bright yellow | Clash / clutter |
579	| Neon green | Neon pink | Clash unless festival/maximalist streetwear |
580	| Black | Charcoal/grey | Good neutral system |
581	| Navy | Burgundy | Good if burgundy repeats once |
582	| Camel | Cream | Good warm-neutral system |
583	
584	```ts
585	function scoreHatAndScarfTogether(
586	  hat: Hat,
587	  scarf: Scarf,
588	  coat: Garment,
589	  outfit: Outfit
590	): number {
591	  const bothStatement =
592	    hat.statementLevel === "statement" &&
593	    scarf.statementLevel === "statement";
594	
595	  if (bothStatement && outfit.register !== "streetwear") return -8;
596	
597	  const sameFamily = colorFamilyMatch(hat.primaryColor, scarf.primaryColor);
598	  const exactMatch =
599	    hat.primaryColor === scarf.primaryColor &&
600	    hat.material === scarf.material;
601	
602	  if (exactMatch) return -1;
603	  if (sameFamily) return 4;
604	  if (hat.statementLevel === "statement" || scarf.statementLevel === "statement") return 3;
605	
606	  return 0;
607	}
608	```

619	| Charcoal coat | Burgundy beanie | Neutral grey scarf | One accent, quiet scarf |
620	| Brown leather jacket | Black cap | Dark-green wool scarf | Dark neutral base + earthy accent |
621

624	| Outer | Hat | Scarf | Problem |
625	|---|---|---|---|
626	| Navy coat | Bright red beanie | Bright yellow scarf | Competing accents |
627	| Camel coat | Camel beanie | Camel scarf | Flat exact matching |

635	
636	# Underwear and Base Layers
637	
638	## Concealment Principle
639	
640	Underwear and base layers are not standard accent accessories. In classic, business, and most casual outfits their default job is to remain invisible.
641	
642	The system should ask:
643	
644	> Is the base layer sufficiently concealed under this garment, without unintended contrast, seams, straps, or show-through?
645	
646	- Under white, light, thin, and semi-sheer garments, nude/beige/taupe/skin-tone base layers are usually least visible.
647	- White underwear under white clothing may show more than nude because white contrasts with skin.
648	- Black, red, and bright underwear under thin white clothing normally creates strong show-through.
649	- Under opaque black, navy, and dark denim clothing, colour is less important if seams and straps remain hidden.[web:155][web:156][web:157][web:158][web:159][web:162][web:164][web:167]
650	
651	```ts
652	type UnderwearRole =
653	  | "bra"
654	  | "bralette"
655	  | "sports_bra"
656	  | "camisole"
657	  | "slip"
658	  | "shapewear"
659	  | "undershirt"
660	  | "tank_base_layer"
661	  | "briefs"
662	  | "boxer_briefs"
663	  | "panties"
664	  | "tights"
665	  | "socks";
666	
667	type VisibilityIntent =
668	  | "hidden"
669	  | "functional_visible"
670	  | "intentional_visible";
671	
672	type Opacity = "opaque" | "medium" | "sheer";
673	type Construction = "seamless" | "flat_seam" | "regular" | "lace" | "ribbed";
674	
675	type Underwear = {
676	  role: UnderwearRole;
677	  color: Color;
678	  material: AccessoryMaterial;
679	  construction: Construction;
680	  opacity: Opacity;
681	  visibilityIntent: VisibilityIntent;
682	  strapVisible?: boolean;
683	  necklineVisible?: boolean;
684	  waistbandVisible?: boolean;
685	  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
686	};
687	```

691	  contrast(underwear.color, nudeFamily) +
692	  contrast(underwear.color, outerGarment.color) +
693	  outerSheerness +
694	  seamVisibility +
695	  exposedStrapOrWaistband;

699

702	  | "light_nude"
703	  | "medium_nude"
704	  | "deep_nude"
705	  | "taupe"
706	  | "beige";
707	```

711	## Women’s Underwear Rules
712	
713	| Outer garment | Good base layer | Penalize | Strength |
714	|---|---|---|---|
715	| White thin tee | Nude/beige/taupe seamless bra | Black/red/bright bra, visible seams | HARD |
716	| White blouse | Nude/skin-tone smooth bra | Black bra, contrast straps, lace under thin fabric | HARD |
717	| White opaque shirt | Nude or smooth white/nude | Black bra visible in movement/light | STRONG |
718	| Light semi-sheer blouse | Nude + seamless/flat seams, optional camisole | Contrast colours, lace, thick seams | HARD |
719	| Black opaque tee | Black/nude/subtle bra | Visible lines/straps under tight fit | PREFERENCE |
720	| Navy/charcoal opaque top | Dark/navy/black or nude | Bright colour under thin fabric | STRONG |
721	| Open-back/strap dress | Intentional visible bra, adhesive/bandeau/special base | Random ordinary straps | HARD |
722	| Mesh/lace streetwear/nightwear top | Visible lingerie allowed if intentional | Accidental utilitarian bra | REGISTER-DEPENDENT |
723	
724	A black bra under a thin white tee or blouse is not accent echo; in normal registers it is a show-through defect.[web:155][web:158][web:162][web:164]

727	
728	## Men’s Undershirt Rules
729	
730	| Outer garment | Recommended undershirt | Penalize | Strength |
731	|---|---|---|---|
732	| White dress shirt | Beige/nude/skin-tone or light-grey deep-V | Black undershirt, visible white crew collar | HARD/STRONG |
733	| White tee | Nude/beige/light-grey low neckline | Black base layer, visible collar line | STRONG |
734	| Light-grey thin tee | Nude/beige/light-grey seamless | Black undershirt | STRONG |
735	| Light-blue dress shirt | Nude/beige/light-grey | Black undershirt under thin fabric | STRONG |
736	| Navy/black/dark denim shirt | Black/navy/dark-grey or nude | Low risk if opaque | PREFERENCE |
737	| Sweater/hoodie/overshirt | Functional neutral base layer | Contrasting collar without intention | PREFERENCE |
738	| Sheer/tight top | Nude/skin-tone seamless undershirt | Contrast colour and thick seams | HARD |
739	
740	Beige/natural/skin-tone undershirts under white shirts are typically less visible than pure white; black is generally highly visible. Light grey is a reasonable fallback.[web:155][web:156][web:161][web:165][web:167]
