742	---
743	
744	## Visible Base Layers
745	
746	```ts
747	type BaseLayerMode =
748	  | "concealed"
749	  | "functional_visible"
750	  | "intentional_visible";
751	```
752	
753	### Concealed
754	
755	Default for classic menswear, business, business casual, formal, and most casual looks. Visible contrast, seams, straps, or waistbands produce penalties.
756	
757	### Functional Visible
758	
759	Examples:
760	
761	- White tank under an open overshirt.
762	- Tank under an open shirt.
763	- Sports bra under an athletic layer.
764	- Visible socks as controlled accent.
765	
766	### Intentional Visible
767	
768	Allowed for streetwear, nightlife, festival, editorial/fashion, mesh/lace layering, bralette-as-top, or explicitly styled visible waistband.
769	
770	Only in this mode may a base layer become a palette/accent participant.
771	
772	```ts
773	if (
774	  outfit.register === "streetwear" &&
775	  underwear.visibilityIntent === "intentional_visible"
776	) {
777	  allowAccentEcho = true;
778	} else {
779	  allowAccentEcho = false;
780	}
781	```
782	
783	### Base Layer Examples
784	
785	| Outfit | Base layer | Result |
786	|---|---|---|
787	| White tee | Nude seamless bra | Good; concealed |
788	| White dress shirt | Beige deep-V undershirt | Good; low visibility |
789	| Navy dress | Black seamless bra | Good; opaque outer hides it |
790	| Open white shirt, streetwear | Black ribbed tank | Good; intentional visibility |
791	| Black mesh top + black cargo pants | Black bralette | Good; tonal intentional visibility |
792	| White thin tee | Black bra | HARD penalty |
793	| White blouse | Red bra | HARD penalty |
794	| White shirt | Black undershirt | HARD/STRONG penalty |
795	| Formal dress | Random visible bra straps | HARD penalty |
796	| Business trousers | Bright visible boxer waistband | HARD penalty |
797	
798	---
799	
800	# Production Scoring
801	
802	## Score Models
803	
804	```ts
805	type AccessoryScore = {
806	  leatherCoordination: number;
807	  metalCoordination: number;
808	  materialFormality: number;
809	  accentEcho: number;
810	  visualClutterPenalty: number;
811	  statementBalance: number;
812	  outerAndBagHarmony: number;
813	  hatScarfOuterHarmony: number;
814	};
815	
816	type BaseLayerScore = {
817	  concealmentScore: number;
818	  colorShowThroughPenalty: number;
819	  seamVisibilityPenalty: number;
820	  exposedStrapPenalty: number;
821	  registerCompatibility: number;
822	  intentionalVisibilityBonus: number;
823	};
824	```
825	
826	```ts
827	function scoreAccessories(outfit: Outfit): AccessoryScore {
828	  const leatherItems = getLeatherFamilyCarriers(outfit);
829	  const visibleMetals = getVisibleMetalItems(outfit);
830	  const accentCarriers = getAccentCarriers(outfit);
831	
832	  return {
833	    leatherCoordination: scoreLeatherFamilies(leatherItems, outfit.register),
834	    metalCoordination: scoreMetalFamilies(visibleMetals, outfit.register),
835	    materialFormality: scoreAccessoryMaterialsAgainstRegister(
836	      outfit.accessories,
837	      outfit.register
838	    ),
839	    accentEcho: scoreAccessoryEcho(accentCarriers, outfit.garments),
840	    visualClutterPenalty: scoreVisualClutter(accentCarriers, outfit.accessories),
841	    statementBalance: scoreStatementBalance(outfit.accessories),
842	    outerAndBagHarmony: scoreBagAndOuterRelation(outfit),
843	    hatScarfOuterHarmony: scoreHatScarfOuterwear(outfit),
844	  };
845	}
846	
847	function scoreUnderwearVisibility(
848	  underwear: Underwear,
849	  visibleGarment: Garment,
850	  register: OutfitRegister
851	): number {
852	  if (underwear.visibilityIntent === "intentional_visible") {
853	    return scoreIntentionalVisibleBaseLayer(underwear, visibleGarment, register);
854	  }
855	
856	  const risk =
857	    getColorShowThroughRisk(underwear.color, visibleGarment.color) +
858	    getOpacityRisk(visibleGarment.opacity) +
859	    getConstructionRisk(underwear.construction) +
860	    getStrapRisk(underwear.strapVisible) +
861	    getNecklineRisk(underwear.necklineVisible) +
862	    getWaistbandRisk(underwear.waistbandVisible);
863	
864	  return -risk;
865	}
866	
867	finalScore =
868	  garmentColorScore +
869	  materialScore +
870	  footwearScore +
871	  accessoryScore +
872	  baseLayerScore;
873	```
874	
875	### Suggested Constants
876	
877	```ts
878	const MAX_BRIGHT_ACCENT_HUES = 2;
879	const MAX_STATEMENT_ACCESSORIES = 1;
880	const MAX_VISIBLE_METAL_FAMILIES = 2;
881	const MIXED_METAL_DOMINANT_SHARE = 0.7;
882	const ACCESSORY_ACCENT_MAX_AREA = 0.15;
883	
884	const LEATHER_MATCH_BONUS_CLASSIC = 10;
885	const LEATHER_CLASH_PENALTY_CLASSIC = 15;
886	const METAL_ECHO_BONUS = 5;
887	const ACCENT_ECHO_BONUS_HIGH = 6;
888	const ACCENT_ECHO_BONUS_LOW = 2;
889	const OVER_ACCESSORISED_PENALTY = 8;
890	const UNDERWEAR_SHOW_THROUGH_HARD_PENALTY = 15;
891	```
892	
893	---
894	
895	## Rule Priority
896	
897	### HARD
898	
899	- Brown shoes with black belt in classic/business.
900	- Black shoes with brown belt in classic/business.
901	- Rubber/NATO sports watch with formal or black-tie outfit.
902	- Strong casual nylon/canvas bag visibly clashing with formal tailoring.
903	- Bright hat + bright scarf + bright bag in classic/business register.
904	- Black/red/bright bra under white thin tee/blouse in concealed mode.
905	- Black undershirt under white thin dress shirt in concealed mode.
906	- Random visible bra straps in formal/business outfit.
907	- Visible bright boxer waistband in business/formal register.
908	
909	### STRONG
910	
911	- Shoes, belt, and leather watch strap should share leather family.
912	- Visible metals should be one family or a controlled 70/30 mixed-metal structure.
913	- Accessory material/formality should align with register.
914	- No more than two strong accent hues.
915	- One main statement accessory.
916	- Hat/scarf weight and material should align with outerwear and season.
917	- A colourful coat should use a neutral or controlled tonal scarf.
918	- Use nude/seamless base layer under thin/light garments.
919	- Avoid visible thick seams, straps, and neckline lines when base layer should be hidden.
920	
921	### PREFERENCE
922	
923	- Cool metal with navy/grey/charcoal/black palette.
924	- Warm metal with camel/tan/brown/rust/olive palette.
925	- Bag echoes outerwear/shoes/belt without exact duplication.
926	- Watch dial creates subtle upper/outer echo.
927	- Glasses echo leather or metal family.
928	- Hat repeats one main outfit colour.
929	- Scarf repeats one controlled accent in shoes/bag/hat/gloves.
930	- Light-grey undershirt as fallback under white/light garments.
931	
932	### CONTESTED / REGISTER-DEPENDENT
933	
934	- Exact bag-to-shoe matching: safe but not required; colour family/undertone/finish coordination is more flexible and current.
935	- Gold + silver: valid when intentional, controlled, and repeated.
936	- Neon hats/scarves: can work in festival, outdoor, or maximalist streetwear.
937	- Visible bralette, lace layer, sports bra, tank top, or boxer waistband: only with explicit streetwear/nightlife/editorial frame.
938	
939	---
940	
941	## Testing Checklist
942	
943	### Accessories
944	
945	- Does footwear leather coordinate with belt leather?
946	- If watch strap is leather, does it coordinate with shoe/belt family?
947	- Does watch material fit the register?
948	- Are visible metals one family or controlled mixed metals?
949	- Is there one or fewer main statement accessories?
950	- Are there two or fewer strong accent hues?
951	- Does the bag blend, echo, or contrast intentionally?
952	- Do scarf and hat support outerwear instead of competing with it?
953	- Is a detected colour match meaningful echo rather than random multi-colour overlap?
954	- Is tonal dressing kept separate from accent echo?
955	
956	### Base Layers
957	
958	- Is base layer intended to be hidden or visible?
959	- If hidden, does its colour minimize show-through under garment colour/opacity?
960	- Are seams, straps, neckline, and waistband concealed?
961	- Is construction suitable for tight, thin, or sheer garments?
962	- If visible, is visibility intentional and compatible with the register?
963	- Does visible base layer count as palette/accent only when `intentional_visible`?
964	
965	---
966	
967	## Final Implementation Decision
968	
969	FitCheck should treat accessories and base layers as structured style objects rather than extra colours.
970	
971	Use independent score components:
972	
973	1. `leatherCoordination`
974	2. `metalCoordination`
975	3. `materialFormality`
976	4. `accentEcho`
977	5. `statementBalance`
978	6. `visualClutterPenalty`
979	7. `outerAndBagHarmony`
980	8. `hatScarfOuterHarmony`
981	9. `concealmentScore`
982	10. `colorShowThroughPenalty`
983	11. `intentionalVisibilityBonus`
984	
985	This preserves existing palette logic and the 3-colour ceiling while modelling real visual roles: neutral hues can become details/echoes; leather items coordinate by family; metals form their own system; bags/scarves/hats can blend, echo, or make one statement; and underwear should normally disappear unless visibility is explicitly intentional and register-appropriate.

## Hat Colour Scoring

| Scenario | Result | Rule strength |
|---|---:|---|
| Hat repeats main outer/upper/lower colour | +3 | PREFERENCE |
| Neutral hat: black/navy/grey/camel | +2 | PREFERENCE |

| Bright unrelated hat | -3 | PREFERENCE penalty |
| Hat tonal to coat, 1–2 tones lighter/darker | +3 | STRONG |

| Contrast hat in same temperature family | +3 | PREFERENCE |

A hat should not be a random spot of colour. It should support the dominant colour or create controlled, connected contrast.[web:175][web:176][web:178][web:180][web:182][web:185][web:186][web:187]

## Hat Material Weight Versus Coat

| Coat | Good hat material | Problematic choice |
|---|---|---|
| Wool overcoat | Wool/cashmere beanie, flat cap, structured wool hat | Thin summer cotton cap |
| Puffer | Knit beanie, technical cap, fleece hat | Formal felt fedora |

Hat fabric weight should match coat weight and season.[web:175][web:176][web:186]

## Scarf and Coat Rules

1. The coat leads the outfit; a bold coat requires a quieter scarf.
2. A slim tailored coat works best with a narrow/medium scarf; puffers and parkas can carry chunkier knit/fleece.
3. Scarf material must align with season and coat formality.
4. An accent scarf works best when it repeats in one other meaningful item: bag, shoes, hat, gloves, or tie.[web:177][web:179][web:181][web:183][web:184]

| Coat type | Recommended scarf | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Trench | Medium Cotton, Silk, Fine Wool | Oversized chunky knit/infinity |
| Wool peacoat | Thin ribbed knit, Wool, Cashmere | Very bulky double wrap |
| Wool overcoat | Cashmere, Fine Wool, structured knit | Fleece/sports scarf/loud novelty knit |
| Puffer | Long flat scarf, Chunky knit, Fleece | Thin silk as a winter layer |
| Parka | Wool, Fleece, Chunky knit | Formal silk in outdoor setting |
| Cape/cocoon | Slender/tucked scarf | Stiff bulky scarf |
| Leather jacket | Fine Wool, Cotton, light knit | Overly formal fur scarf in casual register |
| Denim jacket | Cotton/light Wool/casual knit | Heavy cashmere in warm weather |

| Scenario | Result | Rule strength |
|---|---:|---|
| Scarf 1–2 shades lighter/darker than coat | +4 | STRONG |
| Neutral scarf with neutral coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
| Camel scarf + navy coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
| Grey scarf + camel coat | +3 | PREFERENCE |
| Burgundy/olive/rust scarf repeated in bag/shoes/hat | +5 | STRONG |
| Bright scarf is the single bright accent | +2 | PREFERENCE |
| Bright scarf + bright hat + bright bag | -8 | HARD/STRONG penalty |
| Patterned scarf uses outfit palette | +3 | PREFERENCE |
| Patterned scarf adds 3–4 new colours | -4 | STRONG penalty |
| Colourful coat + neutral scarf | +4 | STRONG |
| Colourful coat + unrelated equally bright scarf | -5 | STRONG penalty |

## Hat and Scarf Together

Only one should be a strong statement accessory in normal classic, business, or smart-casual winter outfits.

| Hat | Scarf | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral/tonal | Bright/patterned but echoed elsewhere | Good |
| Bright/patterned but echoed in shoes | Neutral/tonal | Good |
| Same family, different shades/textures | Good tonal system |
| Exact same colour + material | Flat / overly matched |
| Bright red | Bright yellow | Clash / clutter |
| Neon green | Neon pink | Clash unless festival/maximalist streetwear |
| Black | Charcoal/grey | Good neutral system |
| Navy | Burgundy | Good if burgundy repeats once |
| Camel | Cream | Good warm-neutral system |

```ts
function scoreHatAndScarfTogether(
  hat: Hat,
  scarf: Scarf,
  coat: Garment,
  outfit: Outfit
): number {
  const bothStatement =
    hat.statementLevel === "statement" &&
    scarf.statementLevel === "statement";

  if (bothStatement && outfit.register !== "streetwear") return -8;

  const sameFamily = colorFamilyMatch(hat.primaryColor, scarf.primaryColor);
  const exactMatch =
    hat.primaryColor === scarf.primaryColor &&
    hat.material === scarf.material;

  if (exactMatch) return -1;
  if (sameFamily) return 4;
  if (hat.statementLevel === "statement" || scarf.statementLevel === "statement") return 3;

  return 0;
}
```

### Good Outerwear Combinations

| Outer | Hat | Scarf | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Navy wool overcoat | Grey wool beanie | Light-grey wool scarf | Cool-neutral tonal system |
| Camel coat | Black beanie | Cream cashmere scarf | Warm neutrals + controlled contrast |
| Black puffer | Black beanie | Charcoal chunky scarf | Monochrome winter casual with texture |
| Grey trench | Navy cap | Navy silk/wool scarf | Smart-casual echo system |
| Olive parka | Olive beanie | Mustard wool scarf | Earth-tone system, controlled accent |
| Charcoal coat | Burgundy beanie | Neutral grey scarf | One accent, quiet scarf |
| Brown leather jacket | Black cap | Dark-green wool scarf | Dark neutral base + earthy accent |

### Bad Outerwear Combinations

| Outer | Hat | Scarf | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Navy coat | Bright red beanie | Bright yellow scarf | Competing accents |
| Camel coat | Camel beanie | Camel scarf | Flat exact matching |
| Black coat | Neon green beanie | Neon pink scarf | Conflicting neons |
| Grey coat | Orange beanie | Purple scarf | Unrelated bright accents |
| Slim wool coat | Very bulky scarf | Heavy oversized beanie | Overwhelms silhouette |
| Trench | Heavy fur hat | Chunky knit scarf | Season/material mismatch |
| Formal overcoat | Logo-heavy sports cap | Fleece scarf | Formality mismatch |

---

# Underwear and Base Layers

## Concealment Principle

Underwear and base layers are not standard accent accessories. In classic, business, and most casual outfits their default job is to remain invisible.

The system should ask:

> Is the base layer sufficiently concealed under this garment, without unintended contrast, seams, straps, or show-through?

- Under white, light, thin, and semi-sheer garments, nude/beige/taupe/skin-tone base layers are usually least visible.
- White underwear under white clothing may show more than nude because white contrasts with skin.
- Black, red, and bright underwear under thin white clothing normally creates strong show-through.
- Under opaque black, navy, and dark denim clothing, colour is less important if seams and straps remain hidden.[web:155][web:156][web:157][web:158][web:159][web:162][web:164][web:167]

```ts
type UnderwearRole =
  | "bra"
  | "bralette"
  | "sports_bra"
  | "camisole"
  | "slip"
  | "shapewear"
  | "undershirt"
  | "tank_base_layer"
  | "briefs"
  | "boxer_briefs"
  | "panties"
  | "tights"
  | "socks";

type VisibilityIntent =
  | "hidden"
  | "functional_visible"
  | "intentional_visible";

type Opacity = "opaque" | "medium" | "sheer";
type Construction = "seamless" | "flat_seam" | "regular" | "lace" | "ribbed";

type Underwear = {
  role: UnderwearRole;
  color: Color;
  material: AccessoryMaterial;
  construction: Construction;
  opacity: Opacity;
  visibilityIntent: VisibilityIntent;
  strapVisible?: boolean;
  necklineVisible?: boolean;
  waistbandVisible?: boolean;
  formality: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
};
```

```ts
underwearVisibilityRisk =
  contrast(underwear.color, nudeFamily) +
  contrast(underwear.color, outerGarment.color) +
  outerSheerness +
  seamVisibility +
  exposedStrapOrWaistband;
```

Optional technical field, without storing the user’s personal skin-tone data:

```ts
type UnderwearNudeFamily =
  | "light_nude"
  | "medium_nude"
  | "deep_nude"
  | "taupe"
  | "beige";
```

---

## Women’s Underwear Rules

| Outer garment | Good base layer | Penalize | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| White thin tee | Nude/beige/taupe seamless bra | Black/red/bright bra, visible seams | HARD |
| White blouse | Nude/skin-tone smooth bra | Black bra, contrast straps, lace under thin fabric | HARD |
| White opaque shirt | Nude or smooth white/nude | Black bra visible in movement/light | STRONG |
| Light semi-sheer blouse | Nude + seamless/flat seams, optional camisole | Contrast colours, lace, thick seams | HARD |
| Black opaque tee | Black/nude/subtle bra | Visible lines/straps under tight fit | PREFERENCE |
| Navy/charcoal opaque top | Dark/navy/black or nude | Bright colour under thin fabric | STRONG |
| Open-back/strap dress | Intentional visible bra, adhesive/bandeau/special base | Random ordinary straps | HARD |
| Mesh/lace streetwear/nightwear top | Visible lingerie allowed if intentional | Accidental utilitarian bra | REGISTER-DEPENDENT |

A black bra under a thin white tee or blouse is not accent echo; in normal registers it is a show-through defect.[web:155][web:158][web:162][web:164]

---

## Men’s Undershirt Rules

| Outer garment | Recommended undershirt | Penalize | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| White dress shirt | Beige/nude/skin-tone or light-grey deep-V | Black undershirt, visible white crew collar | HARD/STRONG |
| White tee | Nude/beige/light-grey low neckline | Black base layer, visible collar line | STRONG |
| Light-grey thin tee | Nude/beige/light-grey seamless | Black undershirt | STRONG |
| Light-blue dress shirt | Nude/beige/light-grey | Black undershirt under thin fabric | STRONG |
| Navy/black/dark denim shirt | Black/navy/dark-grey or nude | Low risk if opaque | PREFERENCE |
| Sweater/hoodie/overshirt | Functional neutral base layer | Contrasting collar without intention | PREFERENCE |
| Sheer/tight top | Nude/skin-tone seamless undershirt | Contrast colour and thick seams | HARD |

Beige/natural/skin-tone undershirts under white shirts are typically less visible than pure white; black is generally highly visible. Light grey is a reasonable fallback.[web:155][web:156][web:161][web:165][web:167]

---

## Visible Base Layers

```ts
type BaseLayerMode =
  | "concealed"
  | "functional_visible"
  | "intentional_visible";
```

### Concealed

Default for classic menswear, business, business casual, formal, and most casual looks. Visible contrast, seams, straps, or waistbands produce penalties.

### Functional Visible

Examples:

- White tank under an open overshirt.
- Tank under an open shirt.
- Sports bra under an athletic layer.
- Visible socks as controlled accent.

### Intentional Visible

Allowed for streetwear, nightlife, festival, editorial/fashion, mesh/lace layering, bralette-as-top, or explicitly styled visible waistband.

Only in this mode may a base layer become a palette/accent participant.

```ts
if (
  outfit.register === "streetwear" &&
  underwear.visibilityIntent === "intentional_visible"
) {
  allowAccentEcho = true;
} else {
  allowAccentEcho = false;
}
```

### Base Layer Examples

| Outfit | Base layer | Result |
|---|---|---|
| White tee | Nude seamless bra | Good; concealed |
| White dress shirt | Beige deep-V undershirt | Good; low visibility |
| Navy dress | Black seamless bra | Good; opaque outer hides it |
| Open white shirt, streetwear | Black ribbed tank | Good; intentional visibility |
| Black mesh top + black cargo pants | Black bralette | Good; tonal intentional visibility |
| White thin tee | Black bra | HARD penalty |
| White blouse | Red bra | HARD penalty |
| White shirt | Black undershirt | HARD/STRONG penalty |
| Formal dress | Random visible bra straps | HARD penalty |
| Business trousers | Bright visible boxer waistband | HARD penalty |

---

# Production Scoring

## Score Models

```ts
type AccessoryScore = {
  leatherCoordination: number;
  metalCoordination: number;
  materialFormality: number;
  accentEcho: number;
  visualClutterPenalty: number;
  statementBalance: number;
  outerAndBagHarmony: number;
  hatScarfOuterHarmony: number;
};

type BaseLayerScore = {
  concealmentScore: number;
  colorShowThroughPenalty: number;
  seamVisibilityPenalty: number;
  exposedStrapPenalty: number;
  registerCompatibility: number;
  intentionalVisibilityBonus: number;
};
```

```ts
function scoreAccessories(outfit: Outfit): AccessoryScore {
  const leatherItems = getLeatherFamilyCarriers(outfit);
  const visibleMetals = getVisibleMetalItems(outfit);
  const accentCarriers = getAccentCarriers(outfit);

  return {
    leatherCoordination: scoreLeatherFamilies(leatherItems, outfit.register),
    metalCoordination: scoreMetalFamilies(visibleMetals, outfit.register),
    materialFormality: scoreAccessoryMaterialsAgainstRegister(
      outfit.accessories,
      outfit.register
    ),
    accentEcho: scoreAccessoryEcho(accentCarriers, outfit.garments),
    visualClutterPenalty: scoreVisualClutter(accentCarriers, outfit.accessories),
    statementBalance: scoreStatementBalance(outfit.accessories),
    outerAndBagHarmony: scoreBagAndOuterRelation(outfit),
    hatScarfOuterHarmony: scoreHatScarfOuterwear(outfit),
  };
}

function scoreUnderwearVisibility(
  underwear: Underwear,
  visibleGarment: Garment,
  register: OutfitRegister
): number {
  if (underwear.visibilityIntent === "intentional_visible") {
    return scoreIntentionalVisibleBaseLayer(underwear, visibleGarment, register);
  }

  const risk =
    getColorShowThroughRisk(underwear.color, visibleGarment.color) +
    getOpacityRisk(visibleGarment.opacity) +
    getConstructionRisk(underwear.construction) +
    getStrapRisk(underwear.strapVisible) +
    getNecklineRisk(underwear.necklineVisible) +
    getWaistbandRisk(underwear.waistbandVisible);

  return -risk;
}

finalScore =
  garmentColorScore +
  materialScore +
  footwearScore +
  accessoryScore +
  baseLayerScore;
```

### Suggested Constants

```ts
const MAX_BRIGHT_ACCENT_HUES = 2;
const MAX_STATEMENT_ACCESSORIES = 1;
const MAX_VISIBLE_METAL_FAMILIES = 2;
const MIXED_METAL_DOMINANT_SHARE = 0.7;
const ACCESSORY_ACCENT_MAX_AREA = 0.15;

const LEATHER_MATCH_BONUS_CLASSIC = 10;
const LEATHER_CLASH_PENALTY_CLASSIC = 15;
const METAL_ECHO_BONUS = 5;
const ACCENT_ECHO_BONUS_HIGH = 6;
const ACCENT_ECHO_BONUS_LOW = 2;
const OVER_ACCESSORISED_PENALTY = 8;
const UNDERWEAR_SHOW_THROUGH_HARD_PENALTY = 15;
```

---

## Rule Priority

### HARD

- Brown shoes with black belt in classic/business.
- Black shoes with brown belt in classic/business.
- Rubber/NATO sports watch with formal or black-tie outfit.
- Strong casual nylon/canvas bag visibly clashing with formal tailoring.
- Bright hat + bright scarf + bright bag in classic/business register.
- Black/red/bright bra under white thin tee/blouse in concealed mode.
- Black undershirt under white thin dress shirt in concealed mode.
- Random visible bra straps in formal/business outfit.
- Visible bright boxer waistband in business/formal register.

### STRONG

- Shoes, belt, and leather watch strap should share leather family.
- Visible metals should be one family or a controlled 70/30 mixed-metal structure.
- Accessory material/formality should align with register.
- No more than two strong accent hues.
- One main statement accessory.
- Hat/scarf weight and material should align with outerwear and season.
- A colourful coat should use a neutral or controlled tonal scarf.
- Use nude/seamless base layer under thin/light garments.
- Avoid visible thick seams, straps, and neckline lines when base layer should be hidden.

### PREFERENCE

- Cool metal with navy/grey/charcoal/black palette.
- Warm metal with camel/tan/brown/rust/olive palette.
- Bag echoes outerwear/shoes/belt without exact duplication.
- Watch dial creates subtle upper/outer echo.
- Glasses echo leather or metal family.
- Hat repeats one main outfit colour.
- Scarf repeats one controlled accent in shoes/bag/hat/gloves.
- Light-grey undershirt as fallback under white/light garments.

### CONTESTED / REGISTER-DEPENDENT

- Exact bag-to-shoe matching: safe but not required; colour family/undertone/finish coordination is more flexible and current.
- Gold + silver: valid when intentional, controlled, and repeated.
- Neon hats/scarves: can work in festival, outdoor, or maximalist streetwear.
- Visible bralette, lace layer, sports bra, tank top, or boxer waistband: only with explicit streetwear/nightlife/editorial frame.

---

## Testing Checklist

### Accessories

- Does footwear leather coordinate with belt leather?
- If watch strap is leather, does it coordinate with shoe/belt family?
- Does watch material fit the register?
- Are visible metals one family or controlled mixed metals?
- Is there one or fewer main statement accessories?
- Are there two or fewer strong accent hues?
- Does the bag blend, echo, or contrast intentionally?
- Do scarf and hat support outerwear instead of competing with it?
- Is a detected colour match meaningful echo rather than random multi-colour overlap?
- Is tonal dressing kept separate from accent echo?

### Base Layers

- Is base layer intended to be hidden or visible?
- If hidden, does its colour minimize show-through under garment colour/opacity?
- Are seams, straps, neckline, and waistband concealed?
- Is construction suitable for tight, thin, or sheer garments?
- If visible, is visibility intentional and compatible with the register?
- Does visible base layer count as palette/accent only when `intentional_visible`?

---

## Final Implementation Decision

FitCheck should treat accessories and base layers as structured style objects rather than extra colours.

Use independent score components:

1. `leatherCoordination`
2. `metalCoordination`
3. `materialFormality`
4. `accentEcho`
5. `statementBalance`
6. `visualClutterPenalty`
7. `outerAndBagHarmony`
8. `hatScarfOuterHarmony`
9. `concealmentScore`
10. `colorShowThroughPenalty`
11. `intentionalVisibilityBonus`

This preserves existing palette logic and the 3-colour ceiling while modelling real visual roles: neutral hues can become details/echoes; leather items coordinate by family; metals form their own system; bags/scarves/hats can blend, echo, or make one statement; and underwear should normally disappear unless visibility is explicitly intentional and register-appropriate.

content.text:
Read it in full. My honest assessment:

## What it confirms

Two things land as independent validation, not new work:

**Your palette-class-vs-visual-role rule** (lines 23–42) is exactly what we shipped in `35a4258` — down to the same examples (navy swoosh, camel tab). And lines 435–436 confirm the other half: all-navy and brown-on-brown are "tonal dressing; avoid double count," not echo. Your instinct was right and the research agrees independently.

**Line 455 answers the question I hit twenty minutes ago.** "Grey suit + black shoes/belt + silver watch → palette count 2–3 — silver hardware is normally not garment hue." Our `vocab.ts:76` marks silver non-neutral, with the reasoning "as hardware they rarely reach the tag set" — which was true until you uploaded a watch and a bracelet, both tagged `colors=["silver"]`. That comment's premise is now dead, and the research says how to fix it.

## What's genuinely actionable now

- **Metal system** (`metalTone`: cool/warm/dark). Inferable from a photo, fixes the silver bug, and gives us `metalEcho` — steel watch + silver chain is a real signal we currently score as a colour clash. **High value, low cost.**
- **3-colour ceiling + accessories** (443–457). Directly fixes a live defect.
- **Bag intent** blend/echo/contrast (307–335) — lands right on the bags work we were about to start.

## What's blocked, and it's most of the document

The same wall that stopped the accessory cap: **we don't own the items.** Leather coordination is the document's biggest section and its anchor is the belt — you have no belts. `hatScarfOuterHarmony` needs hats and scarves. Ties, pocket squares, glasses, rings, earrings — none. You own a watch, a bracelet, a clutch and a camera bag.

I'd rather say this now than build nine scoring components that can never fire.

## What I'd cut

**The underwear and base-layer sections (636–797).** I don't think this belongs in Fitcheck, and I'd push back even though you gave me the research:

- Users will not photograph their underwear. The whole system is built on "upload your wardrobe," and this is the one category that won't be uploaded.
- The daily drop shows a visible outfit. Underwear isn't in it.
- Key fields (`strapVisible`, `necklineVisible`, `waistbandVisible`) are **outfit facts, not item facts** — they depend on what's worn over. Our schema tags items in isolation, so these can't be tagged at capture at all.
- It edges toward skin-tone data, which the research itself flags as something to avoid storing.

The narrow piece worth keeping: a visible tank under an open overshirt is a real streetwear move. That's a normal Top, not a new subsystem.

## Two structural notes

**The numbers don't transplant.** The research scores in ±10/±15 points; ours is 0–1 normalised weights. But its **HARD / STRONG / PREFERENCE** ladder maps cleanly onto what we already have: HARD → a filter in `candidates.ts`, STRONG → a high-weight term, PREFERENCE → a low-weight term. That mapping is the useful part, not the constants.

**Agreed on the code** — it assumes an `Outfit`/`register` object model we don't have. Our pipeline is candidates → score → diversity → rerank, and the rules should enter as terms in `score.ts`.

## Where I'd put it in the queue

Ahead of the trios research, behind what's already planned:

1. **Bags + watch + metal system** — one plan. Bags category, metal tone, silver-as-hardware fix, watch reward. Everything here is buildable with the items you own.
2. **Plan 5** — value contrast + texture rescue (fixes the `camel/beige/camel` trap we measured).
3. **Plan 3** — frame detection, rule registry, material/texture matrices.
4. Leather coordination + hat/scarf — **when the closet has belts and scarves**, not before.

Want me to write plan 1 up?

# Bags, Watches and the Metal System — Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make the accessories the user actually owns score correctly. Metal stops being counted as a garment colour, a metal family becomes its own signal, bags get their own slot, and a watch is preferred when it suits the outfit.

**Architecture:** One new category, one derived item property (metal tone), one new scoring term, one small reward. No new tagger question — every input is derived from `material` and `colors`, which the tagger already writes.

**Tech Stack:** TypeScript, Vitest, Supabase/Postgres migration.

**Research:** `docs/research/fitcheck-accessories-and-base-layers-complete-en.md`

**Branch from:** `develop` (PR #62 merged 2026-09-08; `resolveAccent`, `WEARABLE_CATEGORIES` and the two-accessory cap are all there).

## Why this plan exists

The user uploaded four accessories — a quartz watch, a chain bracelet, a Valentino wristlet clutch and a camera bag. Measuring them against the real scorer found two defects and one gap:

| # | Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A silver watch is scored as a **garment colour** | `vocab.ts:84` marks `silver` `neutral: false`. Its own comment justifies this with "as hardware they rarely reach the tag set" — false since the watch and bracelet both tag `colors: ["silver"]` |
| 2 | Adding a well-matched watch makes an outfit **worse** | measured: all-neutral outfit 0.9010 → 0.8930 with a steel watch |
| 3 | Bags share the accessory budget and the same cap | `by.Accessories` is the only optional non-outerwear slot |

The research is explicit on (1): *"Grey suit + black shoes/belt + silver watch → palette count 2–3 — silver hardware is normally not garment hue"* (line 455), and on the general principle: *"treat accessories as structured style objects rather than extra colours"* (line 969).

The penalty half of the watch rule **already works** and must not be touched: a f3 watch against a f5 evening outfit measured 0.9157 → 0.7750, a 0.14 cost from `formalityCoherence` alone. That is the mechanism the product owner asked for — a watch that does not suit gets dropped — and it needs no gender switch, which is deliberate (`womens-wardrobe-gap`: rules key off the garment).

## Global Constraints

- ⚠️ **Every task ends with a re-measurement against the real closet**, not a green suite. Use the user's real rows (`user_id = a8e382e1-faa8-41dd-9ec4-3b4bd47d19fe`), **never a query without a `user_id` filter** — an unfiltered query mixes in the e2e user's 7 fixtures and produced a wrong measurement once already.
- **Return `null`, never `0.5`, when a signal has no evidence** — the `climateFit` contract in `score.ts`.
- Signals may weight, never filter. A closet with no watch, no bag and no metal must produce exactly the outfits it produces today.
- ⚠️ **Check stock before building a rule.** Task 4 of the last plan was a no-op because the closet held zero accessories. Each task below states what it needs and what to do if it is missing.
- ⚠️ **A test written to guard a regression must be proven to fail.** Break the code, watch it go red, revert. Two tests shipped last plan that guarded nothing and passed either way.
- Verification is `npm run test:run`, then `npx tsc --noEmit`, then `npm run build`, then `npm run insights` if a route was touched.

---

### Task 1: Metal is hardware, not a garment colour

**Needs:** at least one item whose material is `Stainless steel`, `Silver` or `Gold`. The closet has two (watch, bracelet). If none, STOP and report.

`colorHarmonyScore` counts distinct non-neutral colours against a three-colour ceiling. `silver` and `gold` are `neutral: false`, so a steel watch spends one of those slots.

⚠️ **The fix keys off the MATERIAL, not the colour.** A silver puffer jacket is a deliberate colour choice and must keep counting; a steel watch case is hardware and must not. Gating on the colour name would break the first case, which is exactly the palette-class-vs-role confusion this codebase has already fixed once for accents.

- [ ] Add `metalTone(material, colors): "cool" | "warm" | "dark" | null` in a new `lib/generator/styling/metal.ts`. Cool: `Stainless steel`, `Silver`, plus `silver`/`grey` on a metal material. Warm: `Gold`, plus `gold`/`bronze`. Dark: a metal material whose colour is `black`/`charcoal`. Returns `null` for any non-metal material — that is the "not hardware" answer and every garment gets it.
- [ ] In `scoreCombo`, exclude an item's colours from the palette count when `metalTone(...)` is non-null. Keep passing them everywhere else untouched.
- [ ] Test: a silver **garment** (material `Polyester`, colour `silver`) still counts toward the ceiling; a silver **watch** (material `Stainless steel`) does not.
- [ ] Measure: the all-neutral outfit + steel watch delta. It is **0.9010 → 0.8930** today; after this it must not fall.

---

### Task 2: A metal system, scored once

**Needs:** two or more metal items in one combo. The closet has exactly two (watch + bracelet, both silver), so the term can fire — but only in combos carrying both.

Research: one visible metal family is the safe default (+10); a four-way mix is a penalty (−8); mixed metals are fine when one dominates and repeats (+5). On our 0–1 scale that is a term, not a filter.

- [ ] `metalCoordination(items): number | null` in `metal.ts`. `null` when fewer than **two** metal items — most outfits, and null is how this codebase says "no evidence".
- [ ] One family across all metal items → 1.0. Two families where one is a clear majority → 0.6. An even split of two or more families → 0.25.
- [ ] Add to `score.ts` as a `PREFERENCE`-strength term. ⚠️ Suggested weight **0.1**, well under `coherence` (0.3): the research ranks metal consistency below formality and register, and a metal clash must never outrank a formality clash.
- [ ] Test the null case explicitly: zero and one metal item both return `null` and the term claims no weight.
- [ ] Measure: confirm watch + bracelet in one combo now scores above the same combo with one of them swapped for a non-metal accessory of equal formality.

---

### Task 3: Bags are their own slot

**Needs:** at least one bag. The closet has two (clutch, camera bag) — but both are currently tagged `Accessories` and must be migrated.

The clutch was verified from its cutout: a black Valentino wristlet with a wrist strap. It is a carried, visible, styled piece — not a billfold — so no visible/invisible concept is needed. Research treats a bag as a possible colour block (line 120), which is the opposite of Task 1's metal rule: **a bag's colours DO count toward the ceiling.**

- [ ] Add `"Bags"` to `TagSchema.category`. Update the tagging prompt so the model knows the category exists and what belongs in it (bags, totes, clutches, backpacks, wallets).
- [ ] Migration: move the two existing rows from `Accessories` to `Bags`, matched on `subcategory`, not on name.
- [ ] `components/closet/closet-grid.tsx` — add the filter chip.
- [ ] `lib/packing/rewear.ts` — add `"Bags"` to `ALWAYS_REWEARABLE`. A bag is carried for a whole trip, not re-picked daily.
- [ ] `buildCandidates` — a bag slot with its own cap, **maximum 1**. ⚠️ **Do not add a third push per iteration.** The accessory cap proved what that costs: a separate variant per base spends the fixed `CAP` of 200 on permutations of the same three garments and stranded 13 of 80 garments in the test. Extend the existing single extras push to choose among {accessory, bag, both} instead.
- [ ] Test: garment reach at `maxBags: 1` equals reach at `maxBags: 0`, on a closet large enough that the cap binds (80 of each — 14 is not enough, the breadth-first walk reaches everything in pass 0 regardless).
- [ ] Measure: combo count and top-10 composition before and after on the real closet.

---

### Task 4: A watch is preferred when it suits

**Needs:** a watch. The closet has one.

Today a watch can only cost. The reward is the missing half; the penalty already exists and must be left alone.

⚠️ **Measured window, do not guess:** a well-matched watch currently costs about **0.008**, a badly-matched one about **0.14**. Any reward between roughly **0.02 and 0.08** therefore includes a watch that fits and still lets a formality clash exclude it. Pick a value in that range and pin both ends in tests.

- [ ] A small positive term for wristwear present in the combo. `null` when the closet contributes no wristwear, so an outfit without one is not penalised — the absence of a watch is not a fault.
- [ ] Test the low end: a f3 watch in a f3 outfit scores **above** the same outfit without it.
- [ ] Test the high end: a f3 watch in a f5 evening outfit scores **below** the same outfit without it. This is the "we don't have another one, so we wouldn't give that watch" case and it is the point of the whole task.
- [ ] ⚠️ Test that nothing keys off gender. The same watch against a f5 dress and a f5 tuxedo must score identically — a gender switch would get the tuxedo wrong.

---

## Explicitly out of scope

- **Leather coordination** (shoes/belt/watch strap). The research's largest section, anchored on the belt. The closet has **no belts**, so every rule would be unfirable. Build it when belts exist.
- **`hatScarfOuterHarmony`.** No hats, no scarves.
- **Ties, pocket squares, socks, glasses, rings, earrings.** None owned.
- **Underwear and base layers** (research lines 636–797). Recommended against: users will not photograph underwear, it never appears in a daily look, and its key fields (`strapVisible`, `necklineVisible`, `waistbandVisible`) are **outfit facts, not item facts** — they depend on what is worn over, so they cannot be tagged at capture, where this codebase tags items in isolation.
- **Bag intent** (blend/echo/contrast) and **statement balance**. Both need a `visualWeight`/`statementLevel` concept that does not exist yet. Worth a later plan once bags are a category.

Checked the DNS. Key thing: **sending and receiving are different problems, and you only have a receiving task.**

**Sending** — nothing to create. Your domain is verified in Resend (DKIM at `resend._domainkey`, Resend's MX + SPF on `send.fitcheck.space`). Any address at a verified domain can be a `From`. `noreply@` and `updates@` need no mailbox — they're just strings in the From header.

**Receiving** — this is the actual work, and only for `support@`, `legal@`, `terms@`. Legal/GDPR contacts must genuinely receive mail. Your MX already points at **Namecheap email forwarding** (`eforward1–5.registrar-servers.com`), so the plumbing exists — you just add the aliases:

> Namecheap → Domain List → fitcheck.space → **Manage → Redirect Email** → add `support`, `legal`, `terms` → forward to your personal inbox.

Free, no mailbox, ~5 minutes. `noreply@` and `updates@` don't need a forwarder.

Two things worth knowing:

1. **Check which domain Resend shows as verified** — root `fitcheck.space` or `send.fitcheck.space`. That decides whether your From is `noreply@fitcheck.space` or `noreply@send.fitcheck.space`. Your root SPF only lists Namecheap forwarding, so if Resend is verified at root, send yourself a test and confirm SPF passes.
2. **DMARC is `p=none`** — monitoring only, anyone can spoof your domain. Once you've confirmed real mail passes, move to `p=quarantine`.

Also: `supabase/config.toml:189` has the production SMTP block commented out — that's local-only, so make sure Resend SMTP is set in the Supabase **dashboard** for prod, or auth emails will come from Supabase's shared sender with its low rate limit.

content.text:
**SMTP password = a Resend API key.** You don't have one to look up — you create it:

> Resend → **API Keys** → Create API Key → name `supabase-auth`, permission **Sending access** → copy it (shown once only) → paste into Supabase's Password field → Save.

If the field already has a value you can't reveal, just create a new key and overwrite it.

**DMARC** — Namecheap → Domain List → fitcheck.space → **Advanced DNS**. You already have a TXT record, so edit it rather than adding a second (two DMARC records = both ignored):

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Type | TXT Record |
| Host | `_dmarc` |
| Value | `v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:legal@fitcheck.space` |

You're safe to go to `quarantine`: your DKIM key sits at `resend._domainkey.fitcheck.space`, which aligns with a `noreply@fitcheck.space` From, so real mail passes.

**Order matters** — do it last:

1. Create the Resend key → save in Supabase
2. Add the Namecheap forwarders (`legal@` must work before you point `rua` at it)
3. Send yourself a real sign-in email, confirm it arrives
4. *Then* change DMARC

One warning: after `quarantine`, anything else sending as `@fitcheck.space` — a Gmail "send as", a newsletter tool — will start going to spam until you add it to SPF.

Yes, that's correct. Make sure it **replaced** the old `p=none` row rather than sitting alongside it — two `_dmarc` records means both get ignored.

**Adding to SPF:** you don't add a second record, you extend the existing one. Your root TXT (host `@`) is:

```
v=spf1 include:spf.efwd.registrar-servers.com ~all
```

New senders go in as another `include:` before `~all`:

```
v=spf1 include:spf.efwd.registrar-servers.com include:_spf.google.com ~all
```

One SPF record per domain, always — two records is a hard fail.

**Resend needs nothing added.** It sends with a Return-Path on `send.fitcheck.space`, which already carries its own SPF record. That's why your mail passes today. You'd only touch root SPF if you later add Google Workspace, a newsletter tool, etc.

lines: -  Fitcheck — magic-link sign-in email.
-  ⚠️ This is the ONLY email the product sends, and for an email sign-up it is the
-  FIRST thing a new user ever sees of the brand. `enable_confirmations = false`
-  in config.toml means there is no separate signup-confirmation step, so this one
-  template serves both new and returning users — verified against the local mail
-  catcher, where a brand-new address and an existing one both received it.
-  ⚠️ THREE email-specific constraints drive every choice below. None of them
-  apply to the app, so do not "modernise" this into app CSS:
-  1. NO SVG. Gmail strips <svg> entirely and Outlook cannot render it. The
-     lockup files are SVG, so the mark is a PNG raster (`email-mark-96.png`,
-     rendered from `fitcheck-mark-on-light.svg` — the variant drawn for light
-     backgrounds, and pure geometry so no font is needed at raster time).
-  2. IMAGES ARE BLOCKED BY DEFAULT in many clients, so the "fitcheck" wordmark
-     is HTML TEXT, not part of an image. The lockup is reconstructed from a mark
-     image plus serif text — which means the brand still reads when images are
-     off, and stays crisp on retina.
-  3. NO FLEXBOX, NO GRID, NO <style> RELIANCE. Tables and inline styles only;
-     Outlook's engine is Word's.
-  ⚠️ LIGHT, not the app's near-black. The Midnight Atelier palette is beautiful
-  on screen and fragile in mail: dark backgrounds break in Outlook desktop and
-  get inverted unpredictably by client dark modes. The brand carries here
-  through the serif, the rust accent and the dark mark tile instead.

+              Header lockup.
+              ⚠️ ABSOLUTE URL, not `{{ .SiteURL }}`. The template variable
+              depends on the Site URL configured in the Supabase dashboard, and
+              a trailing slash there produces `//brand/...`, which Vercel answers
+              with a 308 redirect — Gmail's image proxy does not follow those, so
+              the logo silently breaks. Verified: `//brand/email-lockup.png`

content.text:
My probes aren't conclusive (the server rejects them before answering about the address), so let me reason from the likely causes instead. Three, in order:

**1. The Alias field contains the full address.** If you typed `support@fitcheck.space` in Alias rather than just `support`, Namecheap builds `support@fitcheck.space@fitcheck.space` and nothing ever matches. Check that column shows only `support`.

**2. Gmail silently dropped it.** If you sent *from* the same Gmail account that `support@` forwards *to*, the forwarded copy comes back with the identical `Message-ID` and Gmail deduplicates it — it never appears, no spam folder, no bounce. This is the single most common false alarm with forwarders.

**3. It's in Spam,** or forwarding is still activating — Namecheap can take up to an hour.

The test that removes all three ambiguities: send to `support@fitcheck.space` **from a different provider** than your forwarding destination — your phone on a different account, or ask someone. Then check Spam too.

If that still fails, tell me and I'll dig into whether the MX host is accepting the mailbox at all.

content.text:
Correct — Namecheap forwarding is **receive-only**. Hit Reply in Gmail today and it goes out from `icurafu333@gmail.com`, exposing your personal address and looking unprofessional.

Fix is Gmail's **"Send mail as"**, using Resend's SMTP so you can reply *as* `support@fitcheck.space`. Free, ~10 minutes:

**1.** Resend → API Keys → create a second key, name it `gmail-send-as`, Sending access. (Separate from the Supabase one so you can revoke either independently.)

**2.** Gmail → Settings → **Accounts and Import** → "Send mail as" → **Add another email address**
- Name: `Fitcheck Support`
- Email: `support@fitcheck.space`
- Leave "Treat as an alias" checked

**3.** SMTP screen:
```
SMTP Server: smtp.resend.com
Port:        587
Username:    resend
Password:    <the gmail-send-as key>
TLS
```

**4.** Gmail emails a verification code to `support@fitcheck.space` → your forwarder delivers it to your inbox → paste it in.

Repeat for `legal@` and `terms@` if you want to reply as those too.

Then in Accounts and Import, set **"Reply from the same address the message was sent to"** — so answering something sent to `legal@` automatically goes out as `legal@` without you picking it each time.

DMARC won't be a problem: Resend signs with your DKIM key at the root domain, so mail sent this way passes even at `p=quarantine`.

content.text:
**Create the labels**

Gmail → left sidebar → scroll down → **More** → **Create new label** → name it `Legal`. Repeat for `Support` and `Terms`.

**Route mail into them automatically**

Gmail → Settings (⚙ → See all settings) → **Filters and Blocked Addresses** → **Create a new filter**

| Filter | Field | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | To | `legal@fitcheck.space` |
| 2 | To | `support@fitcheck.space` |
| 3 | To | `terms@fitcheck.space` |

For each: type the address in **To**, click **Create filter**, then tick:
- ☑ **Apply the label** → choose the matching label
- ☑ **Never send it to Spam**
- ☑ **Also apply filter to matching conversations** (catches anything already received)

Click **Create filter**.

The "Never send it to Spam" tick matters more than the label — forwarded mail loses the original SPF alignment, so Gmail is more likely to flag it. That checkbox prevents a real support request from being buried.

Optional: leave **Skip the Inbox** unchecked. With three low-volume addresses you want them in the inbox; archiving them into labels means you'll forget to look.

-- Bags become their own category, separate from worn accessories.
--
-- Carried and worn items behave differently in three mechanisms, and category
-- is how the generator expresses a slot:
--   * cap — you carry one bag, but you can wear a watch AND a bracelet
--   * colour — a bag is a visible colour block and counts against the palette,
--     where a watch case is hardware and does not (see lib/generator/styling/metal.ts)
--   * packing — a bag is carried for a whole trip, not re-picked daily
--
-- ⚠️ The CHECK constraint has to be replaced, not merely extended: it enumerates
-- the categories, so an insert of 'Bags' fails until this runs. Adding the value
-- to TagSchema without this migration would let the app write a row the database
-- rejects, and the failure would surface at the very end of the capture flow,
-- after the upload and the model call have already been paid for.
alter table public.items drop constraint if exists items_category_check;
alter table public.items add constraint items_category_check
  check (
    category = any (
      array['Tops'::text, 'Bottoms'::text, 'Outerwear'::text, 'Shoes'::text,
            'Bags'::text, 'Accessories'::text, 'Fragrance'::text]
    )
  );

-- Move the bags that were captured before the category existed.
--
-- ⚠️ Matched on `subcategory`, which the tagger writes from the photograph, and
-- never on `name`, which the user is free to edit into anything. A rename must
-- not silently re-file a garment.
--
-- ⚠️ Deliberately conservative. It moves only what is unambiguously a carried
-- bag; anything it misses stays an accessory and can be corrected in the edit
-- sheet, which is a smaller harm than dragging a wearable piece out of the
-- accessory slot. 'wallet' is included because a clutch is frequently tagged
-- that way — the local closet's own "Clutch Bag" arrived from the model as
-- "Clutch wallet", and it is a visible carried piece, not a billfold.
update public.items
set category = 'Bags'
where category = 'Accessories'
  and subcategory is not null
  and (
    subcategory ilike '%bag%'
    or subcategory ilike '%clutch%'
    or subcategory ilike '%wallet%'
    or subcategory ilike '%backpack%'
    or subcategory ilike '%tote%'
    or subcategory ilike '%purse%'
    or subcategory ilike '%satchel%'
    or subcategory ilike '%holdall%'
  );

Root cause found, and it's a real modelling bug — not about bags at all.

`colour-table.ts:23` classifies **`black`, `charcoal`, `grey`, `silver`, `white` as "cool."** So your outfit counts:

```
white shirt    → cool
camel trousers → warm
white sneakers → cool
                 = 2 cool vs 1 warm → "cool-dominant", 0.917

+ camel bag    → 2 cool vs 2 warm → "even split", 0.500
```

Adding camel to a camel outfit registers as a **warm/cool clash**. To the eye that outfit has exactly one colour — camel — on a white ground. The file's own comment warns against precisely this: *"including them would manufacture a split that the eye does not see."* White and black do that.

The cream/ivory-vs-white distinction it was built for is real and worth keeping — a cream shoe is warm, a white one isn't. But "not warm" isn't the same as "cool."

**My proposal:** make the achromatics (`white`, `black`, `grey`, `charcoal`) temperature-**neutral** and leave `cream`/`ivory` warm and `navy`/`denim`/`blue` cool. Then white shirt + camel trousers + white sneakers has one warm vote and no cool ones — no opinion — and adding a camel bag makes it unanimously warm rather than a fake tie.

Two reasons to pause before I do it:

1. **It changes every outfit's score**, not just bags. It needs measuring against your whole closet, not just this case.
2. **`grey` is arguable.** In menswear, grey/charcoal genuinely read as the cool palette against camel/brown/rust. Black and white I'm confident about; grey I'd want your view, since you know the clothes.

So — to your actual question: **yes, a badly-scoring bag is already hidden**, and black behaved correctly. But the reason camel looked worse than black is a bug, and it would have quietly made your generator prefer black bags with warm outfits.

Here's the prompt — self-contained, so your designer AI needs no other context:

```
I'm building an outfit-scoring engine for a wardrobe app. I need your judgement
as a stylist on one specific modelling question. Please answer for real clothes,
not colour theory in the abstract.

## How the rule works

Every garment's colour is classified warm, cool, or temperature-neutral.
For each outfit I count garments (not colour tokens — one garment is one vote),
then measure how decisively one temperature dominates:

  - 70/30 or better in one direction  → good, cohesive
  - an even warm/cool split           → unremarkable, neither rewarded nor punished
  - colours marked "neutral" are EXCLUDED from the count entirely, on the
    principle that a colour which leans neither way should not manufacture a
    split the eye does not see

This comes from the rule that warm and cool may mix but one side should lead.

## The problem I hit

My current table classifies the achromatics — black, charcoal, grey, silver,
white — as COOL. That produces this:

  white shirt + camel trousers + white sneakers
    = 2 cool (both whites) vs 1 warm (camel) → reads as "cool-dominant"

  add a camel bag
    = 2 cool vs 2 warm → reads as an even warm/cool CLASH, and the outfit is
      scored lower than the same outfit with a BLACK bag

So the engine prefers a black bag over a camel one with a camel-and-white
outfit. That seems wrong to me: to the eye that outfit has one colour, camel,
on a white ground — and a camel bag picking up camel trousers is a normal,
good move.

## Questions

1. Should white and black cast a full "cool" vote in a warm/cool dominance
   count, or should they be temperature-neutral (excluded)? Argue it as a
   stylist: does a white shirt make an outfit read cool the way a navy shirt
   does?

2. Same question for GREY and CHARCOAL specifically. My instinct is that these
   are different from black and white — in menswear grey/charcoal genuinely
   read as the cool palette against camel/brown/rust. Do you agree, or should
   they also be neutral?

3. Is SILVER a garment temperature at all, or only a metal tone? (I already
   treat metal hardware — watch cases, buckles, chains — as a separate system
   that does not touch the colour palette.)

4. If the achromatics become neutral, an all-black-and-white outfit would have
   NO temperature votes at all and the rule would simply not apply to it. Is
   that the right outcome, or does a monochrome outfit need a different rule?

5. Are there other rows in my table below that you would move? I care most
   about ones that would change everyday outfits, not edge cases.

## My current full table (42 colours)

cool:    black, charcoal, grey, silver, white, stone, navy, indigo, denim,
         blue, sky, teal, sage, forest, mint, burgundy, purple, lavender, plum
warm:    ivory, cream, sand, beige, khaki, camel, tan, caramel, chocolate,
         brown, olive, maroon, red, rust, terracotta, coral, mustard, yellow,
         gold, orange
neutral: taupe, green, pink

Notes on choices already made, so you know what's deliberate:
  - ivory and cream are warm (white with yellow undertones), plain white is not
  - stone is cool: a pale grey-beige, the coolest of an otherwise-warm family
  - taupe is neutral: a grey-brown between warm beige and cool grey
  - unqualified "green" is neutral because it spans both undertones
  - olive is warm (yellow-based), sage cool (grey-green), forest cool (blue-based)
  - burgundy cool (purple undertone), maroon warm (brown undertone)
  - pink is neutral because it is shade-dependent

## What I need back

- A direct answer to each question, with your reasoning.
- Any rows you would change, as: colour → warm/cool/neutral, plus one line of why.
- Flag anything where stylists genuinely disagree, rather than picking a side to
  sound decisive. I would rather mark a colour neutral than encode a guess.
```

One note: don't let them rewrite the whole table casually. Every row change moves every outfit's score, so I'll measure any accepted change against your real closet before it ships.

1	# FitCheck Temperature Dominance — Stylist Judgment for Men's and Women's Outfits
2	
3	## Question Being Evaluated
4	
5	FitCheck classifies each garment colour as `warm`, `cool`, or `temperature-neutral`. It counts **garments**, not colour tokens: each garment is one vote. The current scoring rule is:
6	
7	- 70/30 or stronger warm/cool dominance -> cohesive.
8	- Even warm/cool split -> no reward and no penalty.
9	- `temperature-neutral` colours are excluded from the temperature count.
10	
11	The original design intent is sound: warm and cool colours may mix, but an outfit often looks more deliberate when one temperature family leads.
12	
13	The modelling question is whether achromatics (`black`, `charcoal`, `grey`, `silver`, `white`) should cast full cool votes, and whether this logic holds for **women's outfits as well as men's outfits**.
14	
15	## Short Decision
16	
17	For both men's and women's wardrobes, FitCheck should use **temperature-neutral** for `black`, `white`, `charcoal`, `grey`, and `silver` in the warm/cool dominance count. They may still be visually powerful colours, high-contrast colours, formal colours, or dominant colour blocks, but they should not manufacture a cool vote.
18	
19	A white shirt or white blouse does not make an outfit visually cool in the same way a navy shirt, cobalt sweater, or steel-blue coat does. Black, white, and grey generally act as achromatic grounds that allow warm or cool hues around them to lead.[web:189][web:194][web:195][web:196][web:201]
20	
21	This recommendation applies equally to women and men. The garment types differ (dress, skirt, trousers, blouse, coat, bag, heels, sneakers), but achromatic colours still operate as neutral grounds in both wardrobes.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Why Garment Voting Is Reasonable
26	
27	Counting garments rather than colour tokens is a good starting model because a visible colour on a top, trouser, dress, coat, shoe, bag, or scarf has different visual impact from a tiny logo or zipper detail.
28	
29	However, a production system should eventually weight garments by role and visible area. A camel overcoat or long dress can visually outweigh a white sneaker even though both are technically one garment. Use garment-count voting now, but preserve a future path to `visibleAreaWeight` or role weights.
30
